about: Every artifact copied into artifacts/ of this repository and of OpenSpineConsortium/symphony-template, read as a file on 2026-10-22 by the thread "Artifact Textbook" (issue #120): what each one is, when it is from, the question it answers, its claims with a grade hint, its numbers with their units, the datasets, tools and models it names, its decisions, its open questions and the artifacts it relates to. Each record was written by a reader that saw only the artifact's own text, as data and never as instructions, and quoted it as evidence; nothing was filled from memory. No e-mail address, phone number or home address is reproduced, and people are named by role.

artifacts.title: AIDaS Seed Grant Proposal
artifacts.readme_summary: Seed grant proposal, 2026-2027 cycle: exact intraoperative vertebral counting on the hospital's own C-arm, closing the domain gap with in-domain fluoroscopy, phantom, cadaver and shadow-mode validation
artifacts.date_evidence: No authoring date is stated. The header names the "2026–2027 Cycle" and the submission is due "by October 16, 2026, 11:59 p.m. ET", so the draft precedes that date; the latest date mentioned is the project end, December 31, 2027.
artifacts.question: What seed project would validate exact intraoperative vertebral counting on the hospital's own C-arm in 2027, and what preliminary results, budget and federal pathway support it?
artifacts.summary: A seed grant proposal for the AIDaS 2026–2027 cycle requesting $20,000 for calendar 2027 to validate exact intraoperative vertebral counting on the C-arm the hospital already owns. It motivates the work with registry, survey, litigation and cost figures on wrong-level spine surgery and argues that the safeguards in use are themselves counts. The method counts rather than names: an anchored first exposure at the sacrum or C2, the C-arm stepped one field minus two bodies, overlapping frames linked by normalised cross-correlation within 0.6 of a body of the commanded step, and a vertebral-body and anchor detector as the only learned component, with a physics renderer of fluoroscopy from CT for training. Preliminary results report exact counts on 99.17–100 % of reached walks and identify detection, not counting, as the deployment risk (99.14 % per-body recall on real films vs 71.67 % render-only), with the renderer explaining 80.9 % of real-frame variance on DeepFluoro. The 2027 plan runs an IRB-approved retrospective fluoroscopy corpus, phantom sweeps, cadaver validation, a Jetson-based frame-grabber prototype, a shadow-mode operating-room study and an FDA pre-submission, leading to an NIH NIBIB R21; the faculty PI slot, several cover-page facts and budget lines 1 to 5 are flagged to confirm.

key_claims.claim: Wrong-level spine surgery persists because a C-arm shows a few vertebrae at a time and the surgeon counts from whatever landmark is visible.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Wrong-level spine surgery persists because a C-arm shows a few vertebrae at a time and the surgeon counts from whatever landmark is visible.

key_claims.claim: In a registry of 34,544 degenerative spine operations the wrong-level incidence was 0.12 %, with intraoperative disorientation the cause in 81.3 %.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the incidence was 0.12% (95% CI 0.09–0.16) ... Intraoperative disorientation was the cause in 81.3% (Furuya et al., Bone Joint J 2026)

key_claims.claim: The safeguards in use are themselves counts; site-verification protocols failed to prevent about one-third of cases.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The safeguards in use are themselves counts. Site-verification protocols failed to prevent about one-third of cases in the one study that assessed them

key_claims.claim: Avoiding the count with preoperative fiducials costs about an hour and 183 mGy each, about $1,750–1,950 of operating-room time per placement.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: at a mean of 51.9 min and 183 mGy each (Siminski et al., AJNR 2023). At $33.78–37.45 per operating-room minute ... that is $1,750–1,950 per placement

key_claims.claim: No verified capital cost for a navigation suite, no study showing navigation reduces wrong-level surgery, and no measure of surgeon workload with versus without navigation are known.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Also not known: a verified capital cost for a navigation suite, any study showing that navigation reduces wrong-level surgery

key_claims.claim: The innovation is to count, not name: the only learned component is a detector, nothing learned decides the level, and there is no tracker, reference frame, preoperative CT or capital equipment.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The innovation is to count, not name. ... The only learned component is a detector of vertebral bodies and the anchor class. Nothing learned decides the level

key_claims.claim: On public labelled CT renders and real radiographs the count was exact on 99.17–100 % of reached walks in twelve arms.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the count was exact on 99.17–100% of reached walks in twelve arms of 16–801 spines (1.13–2.96 exposures per walk)

key_claims.claim: The deployment risk is detection, not counting: a render-only detector reaches 71.67 % per-body recall against 99.14 % for one trained on real films, and exactness falls from 100 % to 30.06 % with its boxes.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The deployment risk is detection, not counting. A detector trained on real films reaches 99.14% per-body recall on real radiographs; the same architecture trained on renders only reaches 71.67%

key_claims.claim: On DeepFluoro the renderer explains 80.9 % of a real frame's variance, nine calibrated device terms add 4.3 points, and a per-frame smooth field reaches 93.9 % against a 99.5 % quantum-noise ceiling.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: our renderer explains 80.9% of a real frame's variance; nine calibrated device terms add 4.3 points, held out by specimen; a per-frame smooth field reaches 93.9% against a 99.5% quantum-noise ceiling

key_claims.claim: A detector trained only on calibrated renders of DeepFluoro's own CTs finds the sacrum on about 96–98 % of real frames; trained on renders of living whole-body CTs it reaches about 64–77 %.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: finds the sacrum on about 96–98% of real frames (leave-one-specimen-out). Trained on renders of living whole-body CTs it reaches about 64–77% depending on round

key_claims.claim: Synthetic fluoroscopy from CT is close in physics but tuned to one C-arm and one cadaveric population, so in-domain real fluoroscopy is required.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: synthetic fluoroscopy from CT is close in physics but tuned to one C-arm and one cadaveric population. The number that matters ... requires in-domain real fluoroscopy

key_claims.claim: The existing Not Human Participant Research determination covers public de-identified data only, so the retrospective fluoroscopy review needs a new IRB protocol.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The existing Not Human Participant Research determination 2026_269 covers public de-identified data only, so this is a new protocol.

key_claims.claim: FDA clearance is not achievable within 2027 from a seed grant; the deliverable is a validated prototype, in-domain data and the pre-submission.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: FDA clearance is not achievable within 2027 from a seed grant. The deliverable is a validated prototype, in-domain data and the pre-submission.

key_claims.claim: The method runs on the C-arm every hospital already owns and can reach community and rural operating rooms without a navigation suite.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the method runs on the C-arm every hospital already owns and needs no capital equipment, no preoperative CT and no tracker, so it can reach community and rural operating rooms

artifacts.title: Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol
artifacts.readme_summary: WSU IRB eProtocol draft (mirrors IRB-21-10-4123): retrospective collection of intraoperative fluoroscopy from DMC spine surgery
artifacts.date_evidence: The form itself says "Date Submitted: Draft" and carries no date of its own. The latest dates it mentions are the planned AIDaS grant period "starting January 1, 2027" and the proposed start "[to confirm: target January 2027]"; the latest past-dated events it cites are the AIDaS deadline "October 16, 2026" and the WSU IRB determination "2026_269, September 2, 2026".
artifacts.question: What does the draft WSU IRB eProtocol say, field by field, for retrospectively collecting archived DMC intraoperative fluoroscopy to fine-tune and test the vertebral-body detector of the level-counting method, and why is Expedited Category 5 requested?
artifacts.summary: A draft WSU IRB eProtocol, mirroring the print view of a precedent protocol (IRB-21-10-4123), for the retrospective collection of archived intraoperative C-arm still images and cine loops from spine operations by one DMC neurosurgeon between 2021 and 2026, to fine-tune and test the vertebral-body detector at the front of the owner's level-counting method in the domain where it would be used. It fills every form section: the checklist (FDA-support box checked, waiver of consent, DMC ancillary review, PHI with a waiver of authorization), funding (none; an AIDaS seed grant application planned), the lay summary, three aims and three hypotheses, a background of cited wrong-level surgery rates and costs, the method under study, inclusion and exclusion, a patient-level split with a sealed test set, a primary endpoint of per-body detector recall (about 1,100 labelled bodies for 97% recall at a 1-point half-width) with secondary count-exactness, decline, agreement and failure endpoints, procedures in order, confidentiality, HIPAA identifiers and attachments. An attached protocol document argues for Expedited Category 5 over Exempt Category 4 and outlines a separate planned follow-on prospective shadow-mode study (Protocol 2) that is not part of this submission. Many fields are marked [to confirm], pending a pilot PACS query, the PI decision and institutional requirements.

decisions.decision: Request Expedited review, Category 5, rather than Exempt Category 4; the Exempt paragraphs are completed only in case the IRB disagrees.
decisions.reason: Research that may support an FDA 510(k) pre-submission is not eligible for exemption; a coded master list is retained during abstraction; the team handles identifiable images with burned-in text; cine loops are clinical video; expedited review yields an approval rather than a concurrence.

decisions.decision: Check the FDA checklist box: data may be included in a future 510(k) pre-submission; no device is used on any participant.
decisions.reason: The data from this retrospective study may support a future FDA submission.

decisions.decision: Request a waiver of consent and a waiver of HIPAA authorization.
decisions.reason: Minimal risk, archived records only, up to N patients over five years many no longer in follow-up; consent would bias the data set toward patients still in contact with the institution.

decisions.decision: Split cases by patient, never by frame; draw and seal a fixed held-out test set before any training; freeze analysis code before fine-tuning.
decisions.reason: So that every case receives a prediction from a model that did not train on it and the primary endpoint is measured on sealed data.

decisions.decision: Restrict to a single neurosurgeon's cases at the DMC over a five-year window.
decisions.reason: A single surgeon gives consistent operative-note documentation of the localisation technique and the operated level, the reference standard; five years reaches the target case count and spans the C-arm units in use.

decisions.decision: Include cervical, thoracic and lumbar cases; include prior instrumentation and transitional anatomy as subgroups; exclude children and identifiable prisoners; do not exclude pregnant patients.
decisions.reason: Performance differs by region and must be reported per region; paediatric morphology differs; prisoners are not a target population; images were acquired for care and pregnancy status is not abstracted.

decisions.decision: Retain year of surgery, C-arm manufacturer and model and acquisition parameters; remove device serial numbers, mask burned-in text on every frame, and hold the master list separately on DMC CITRIX.
decisions.owner: the owner (holder of the master list)
decisions.reason: Failure characterisation by C-arm model needs manufacturer and model; serial numbers are HIPAA identifiers.

decisions.decision: No prospective study is started until detector performance on the institution's own machines and patients is known.
decisions.reason: The deployment risk is the detector and synthetic fluoroscopy does not close the domain gap.

decisions.decision: The follow-on prospective shadow-mode study (Protocol 2) is not part of this submission and will be submitted separately if Protocol 1 meets its endpoints.
decisions.reason: Its prerequisites (Protocol 1 endpoints, phantom sweeps, cadaveric validation, biomedical engineering approval) are not yet met.

decisions.decision: Share only aggregate results; any future release of de-identified images goes to the IRB as an amendment first.
decisions.reason: Confidentiality; no outside sharing is planned.

decisions.decision: Plan an internal AIDaS Seed Grant application; no external funding at submission.
decisions.reason: The Funding section will be amended if awarded.

artifacts.question: Which fluoroscopy, spine radiograph, paired CT-X-ray, CBCT projection and DRR datasets exist for intraoperative vertebral level identification, which are already on the grid, which need a request letter, and which ten gaps are worth getting next?
artifacts.summary: An interactive catalog, as of 17 October 2026, of 217 datasets (189 from the project's own records, 28 found only on the web) sorted into seven kinds (fluoroscopy video, C-arm frames, paired CT and real X-ray, CBCT projections, paired CT and synthetic DRR, radiographs, by request only), each with anatomy, size, annotation level, level labels, pose, access, licence, grid path and notes, and a status: held on the grid (52), request ready (16) or not held (149). A 'Worth getting next' list ranks ten gaps by value to CT-to-C-arm parity (COVID-19-NY-SBU, LUMOS, MIDRC, Balgrist, UCLA kV/MV, PENGWIN, SyntheX, SPARE, LIDC-IDRI, a femur set). Sixteen request letters are ready, eleven also as unsent Outlook drafts; Radiopaedia's seven multi-frame cases are the most appealing but carry a reported USD 250 fee, non-commercial terms and a ban on scripted downloading. A checklist before sending covers commercial use, IRB, training promises, co-authorship and YouTube copies. The entries also record defects in the project's own banks (duplicate persons across splits, wrong row spacing, unused real frames).

artifacts.question: How does a SchwingNet run start on the Wayne State grid without the owner typing a command, what does each job wait for, and what still stands in the way?
artifacts.summary: A private status page for SchwingNet's grid pipeline on 21 October 2026. The gate words are written and under review in SchwingNet PR #54 and no job has run yet; every number so far comes from synthetic CPU runs. A run starts when Claude, from a cloud session, sends one gate word through symphony-template's grid-accounts.yml to the Beethoven gate on the login node, which runs grid/gate.sh, submits Slurm jobs and returns at most 200 kB on the branch grid; one press by the owner remains, Connect GitHub Actions in Beethoven once beethoven-extension #23 reaches him. The start word submits the whole dependency graph (weights, C-ArmLSpine ingest, first catalog, version 1 on GPU, setup when pixi.lock changed, the multi-day X-ray and CT fetch chains, a disk probe), and seven words are everything Claude can ask. Counts are tabled: 111 registry sources by reach, 86 spine-datasets records by status, 22 training registry entries without a shard, 5 of 20 bank recipes ready, fetch list sizes including CT-RATE's 21.3 TB switched off. A schedule runs to the provisional on 30 October and the CNS talk on 2 November, and a ledger lists what waits on the owner, Claude, PhysioNet, Radiopaedia and JHU.

artifacts.readme_summary: Every dataset: what it is, its level truth, how far it reaches (one record per source)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line: 'SchwingNet, data/sources, 60 records, rendered 2026-10-20'.
artifacts.question: What does each of the 60 dataset sources recorded under SchwingNet's data/sources hold, what vertebral level truth does it carry, and how far does the project reach it (held, to get, gated, embargoed, nonexistent or excluded)?
artifacts.summary: A rendered registry of the 60 source records under SchwingNet's data/sources, one row per dataset, grouped as real intraoperative fluoroscopy stills, video and cine, projections with a registered CT, plain films, CT collections and renders, and future directions. Each row gives what the source is, its level truth, a reach word (HAVE, GET, GATED, EMBARGOED, NONE, EXCLUDED), a status, the records' counts, and on opening the licence, the link, the grid path, the steps to get what is not held and the spine-program record it was taken from. The page says its numbers are the records' numbers, that the Markdown page under docs/research is rendered from the same files, and that sample-level counts stay empty until a grid job runs on the owner's word. By my tally of the records, 24 are held on the grid, 22 are to get, 10 are gated, one is embargoed, one does not exist publicly and two are excluded; many of the to-get video sources are requests drafted in September 2026 and never sent.

artifacts.title: OR Readiness Ledger
artifacts.readme_summary: Can it count vertebrae in an operating room it has never seen: what the overnight program measured, refuted and left running
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line: "Fluoroscopic level identification · adversarial readiness program · 2026-09-22 06:10 EDT"; a later re-score is stamped "Re-scored 06:50 EDT".
artifacts.question: Can SchwingNet's fluoroscopic level identification count vertebrae in an operating room (a C-arm device) it has never seen, and what did the overnight adversarial readiness program measure, refute and leave running?
artifacts.summary: A page built at 06:10 EDT on 2026-09-22 from files read on the grid under or_ready/, reporting an overnight program of audits on SchwingNet's level identification. On the device it was trained on, level naming on real OR laterals reaches 98.2% exact level whole-frame (five-fold CV over 148 C-ArmLSpine cases, 95% CI 95.7 to 100), 92.9% with three vertebrae in field and 72.8% with one, with zero leakage pairs found against 37,165 films, 29,484 FluoroCap panels and 1,445 yolo_v6f images. On a device held out entirely the detector finds 83.9% of sacra and 90.6% of vertebrae on whole frames once truth boxes share one convention; the 5.2% in the overnight table was vertebral-body boxes scored against whole-vertebra outline predictions, and the re-score at 06:50 fixed it, while magnified three- and one-vertebra crops stay at 36% and 19%. The page rules the 100% DeepFluoro sacrum number not the manuscript's method, since its render init saw 44.8% of the test specimen's poses and its device terms were fitted on that specimen's real frames; the clean render-only number is 88.5 to 91.3%. Corruption robustness (408 rows), cross-population naming on COBRA and DeepFluoro (a zero-shot level model at 89 to 90% beats the C-ArmLSpine fine-tune's 43.5%), thoracic detection on 608 AASCE films (97 to 99% per level), a SpineSAC six-C-arm sawbone sheet with no truth, device cards for physics styling (styled frames not yet inside the real domain), and a status table of done, running, dead and never-started tracks follow, ending with what the evidence supports, what it does not (counting-grade detection on a fully held-out device, C2 on real images, the styling claim) and next steps with likelihood and impact.

key_claims.claim: On the device it was trained on, level naming on real OR laterals is 98.2% exact whole-frame, cross-validated, with truth independent of the model and no leakage found.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 98.2% exact level on whole C-ArmLSpine lateral frames, five-fold CV over 148 cases [95.7–100]; 92.9% with three vertebrae in the field, 72.8% with one

key_claims.claim: No test frame is in any training corpus: zero near-duplicate pairs against every external corpus, splits disjoint by case.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 0 pairs ≥ 0.97 against 37,165 film images, 29,484 FluoroCap panels, 1,445 yolo_v6f

key_claims.claim: A detector that never saw the C-ArmLSpine C-arm finds 91% of its vertebrae and 84% of its sacra on whole frames; the overnight 5.2% was a box-convention artefact.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Re-scored 06:50 EDT: the 5.2% was a box convention. Under the matched convention the C-ArmLSpine-held-out vertebra recall is 90.6%.

key_claims.claim: Held-out recall collapses on magnified crops: 36% on a three-vertebra field (64% at conf 0.05) and 19% on one vertebra, while the same-device control keeps 82%; scale is a device-transfer lever of its own.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On whole frames the held-out detector is at 91%; on a magnified three-vertebra field it is at 36% (64% at conf 0.05) and on one vertebra 19%.

key_claims.claim: The 100% DeepFluoro sacrum number is not the manuscript's method: the same-device detector was initialised from a render model whose renders were 44.8% under the test specimen's poses and whose device terms were fitted on its real pixels.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The 100% DeepFluoro sacrum number is not the manuscript's method. It is a same-device detector (five specimens' real frames in training) initialised from a render-only model

key_claims.claim: Sacrum found on C-ArmLSpine is partly a statement about layout: a fixed median box hits the truth sacrum on 85.7% of test frames; vertebra recall and level accuracy are not explained this way.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A fixed box (the training set's median sacrum box) hits the truth sacrum at IoU ≥ 0.5 on 85.7% of C-ArmLSpine test frames (median IoU 0.69), 58.5% of COBRA and 13.5% of DeepFluoro.

key_claims.claim: The pipeline degrades gracefully under quantum noise to 300 photons, read noise to sigma 0.06, rotation to 15 degrees, and any gamma, magnification, obliquity, collimation, shutter or instrument in the tested range, costing under 10% of sacrum recall; inversion and a 180 degree flip break every detector at once.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Inversion and a 180° flip break every detector at once (orientation is assumed, not inferred).

key_claims.claim: A level model that never saw a device names 89 to 90% of COBRA lateral levels exactly, and fine-tuning the level model on one device costs it the others (43.5% versus 79.9% with oracle boxes).
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On COBRA laterals the C-ArmLSpine fine-tune scores 43.5% with oracle boxes where the zero-shot model scores 79.9%; the same overfit the detectors showed.

key_claims.claim: Sacrum-anchored counting reaches 80 to 84% on a held-out device, and applies to DeepFluoro's AP pelvis frames where the crop prototype does not.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The crop prototype does not apply to DeepFluoro's AP pelvis frames (few lumbar bodies in field); counting from the sacrum does, at 84.3% device-held-out.

key_claims.claim: C2 on a real image is not demonstrated in any arm: the real-trained arm finds 0 to 8% of 25 labelled C2 instances; render-trained arms find 85 to 88% on renders and none on film.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: C2 on a real image is not demonstrated. The real-film corpus holds 25 labelled C2 instances in val + test and the real-trained arm finds 0–8% of them

key_claims.claim: Thoracic detection on real radiographs is at counting grade per level (97 to 99%) with the film keypoint detector; chains break on L5 and on one missed mid-thoracic body.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Chains break on L5 and on one missed mid-thoracic body, not on the upper thoracic spine.

key_claims.claim: Counting-grade (97% or better) detection on a device held out entirely is not supported yet.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Counting-grade (≥97%) detection on a device held out entirely: best clean numbers are 84% sacrum / 91% vertebrae (C-ArmLSpine), 88–91% sacrum (DeepFluoro render-only, three seeds), 18–50% (COBRA), 32% (image intensifier).

key_claims.claim: Physics-styled synthetic frames are not yet statistically inside the real domain, so that claim is not made.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Real-vs-styled distances on the Cios card: NPS 0.111 against a real-vs-real floor of 0.015; grey histogram 3.1 vs 0.14

key_claims.claim: The SpineSAC sawbone sheet is not a number to quote: TotalSegmentator finds no bone in the sawbone CT, so there is no projected truth and the table counts boxes.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A sawbone with beads is not a patient, and without truth this is a sheet to look at, not a number to quote.

key_claims.claim: Two denominators are in circulation for DeepFluoro vertebra truth: 83 kept versus all 312 boxes; the loader is fixed but the whole-spine curves still use 312.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: test split carries 83 kept and 229 dropped (out-of-field) boxes; older evaluations scored recall against all 312. Fixed in realxray_eval.load_truth

key_claims.claim: The device-card fit reproduces the shipped DeepFluoro calibration folds to 1e-3 per term.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The fit reproduces the shipped DeepFluoro calibration folds to 1e-3 per term.

artifacts.title: Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy
artifacts.readme_summary: Counting the vertebral level under fluoroscopy without a tracker, prepared for Dr. Chou and the department
artifacts.date_evidence: Header chip: "Proposal · intraoperative level counting · September 2026". The latest dated item is the run stamp: "Every synthetic-data number here is from the leave-one-specimen-out runs of 21 September 2026".
artifacts.question: Can the vertebral level be counted under C-arm fluoroscopy without a tracker, how exact is the count given correct boxes, where does synthetic training data stop, and what would retrospective in-house fluoroscopy let the method guarantee?
artifacts.summary: A proposal prepared for a department spine surgeon and the department: count the level from an anchor the surgeon trusts (sacrum or C2) along a C-arm sweep, with the only learned stage a detector of vertebral bodies and the anchor, frames linked by normalised cross-correlation into a chain, and the target read as the k-th node; no name such as L4 is ever formed. On public CT renders and real radiographs the count is exact on 99.17 to 100% of walks across twelve arms (16 to 801 spines each), and the film-trained detector reaches 99.14% per-body recall on real films against 71.67% for a renders-only one. Synthetic fluoroscopy from CT was calibrated on DeepFluoro (366 frames, six cadaveric pelves): physics explains 81% (86% once the log-compressed display is read correctly) of a real frame's variance and the calibrated renderer 93.9% in attenuation space, yet a detector trained on living whole-body CT renders finds the sacrum on only 64 to 77% of real frames against 90 to 97% when trained on the test population's own CTs, and learned refiners add eight to ten points inside a 26-point seed spread. The proposal therefore asks for five years of the surgeon's own PACS fluoroscopy (2021 to 2026) under a retrospective protocol, annotation of a subset by a resident, and a measured bound on wrong-level output at a chosen decline rate, plus an immediate start on the WSU C-arm with a phantom and a cadaver. Wrong-level surgery is framed as 1 in 830 operations and 81% of events a count gone wrong under fluoroscopy.

artifacts.title: Counting From The Sacrum
artifacts.readme_summary: Counting from the sacrum, Wayne State, 22 September 2026 (with its figure fig1_story.png)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Wayne State · 22 September 2026' and the section 'What today's audit found'.
artifacts.question: Does naming the vertebral level from C-arm exposures alone, by counting from the sacrum with no CT, tracker or registration, beat the published literature, and what did the 22 September 2026 audit of the synthetic-data pipeline find?
artifacts.summary: A one-page report of the registration-free level-naming method (expose, detect, link, chain, count, confirm; only the shaded boxes learned) with the figure fig1_story.png, stating that every number is verified against a file on disk (docs/RSNAI_CLAIMS.json, 54 claims). On naming it claims a wide lead: 98.22% exact level on real intraoperative lateral C-arm frames (141 cases, 617 vertebrae, 5-fold CV; 100% within one; 95% case-bootstrap lower bound 95.71%), 96.67% AP, 96.27% zero-shot lateral with no C-ArmLSpine data in training, and 99.87% (n 3,720) on CSXA cervical and 98.04% (n 2,698) on BUU-LSPINE plain radiographs, against a best published registration-free 73.3% that imports identity from a preoperative radiograph and LevelCheck, which needs the patient's CT. On detection it concedes the binding constraint: 90.6% per-body recall on a held-out device against published 0.96–0.98, and a render-only detector at 71.7% on real radiographs versus 99.1% trained on real film. The audit found the C-arm cards do sample fitted distributions (51 of 114 device-parameter pairs from a Gaussian copula conditioned on water-equivalent thickness), but a clip on 8–11 correlated terms saturates rather than truncates, so renders reached only 1.7–5.1% of the joint with 94.9–98.3% of frames carrying a pinned term; a replacement sampler reaching 99% is implemented but not adopted pending an A/B. The CT axis was re-counted by distinct subject (TotalSegmentator v3 1,735, v2 1,170, CTSpinoPelvic1K 801, VerSe 374, C-ArmLSpine 120). Open: whether a CTSpinoPelvic1K release id is one person (prone and supine colonography), a fleet-wide detector training now (18,906 frames, 56 test specimens), and 2,654 frames of vendor kilovoltage on disk unused.

artifacts.question: How does the counting rule R + C = 22 flag a vertebral column with an extra or missing vertebra, and what can counting alone not tell?
artifacts.summary: An interactive design (one board, R + C = 22) that explains the vertebral count anomaly rule: C1 is excluded from these datasets, so an ordinary column holds 23 vertebrae (C2 to C7, T1 to T12, L1 to L5), and for any target vertebra the count above it (R, rostral) plus the count below it (C, caudal) must be 22, with the sacrum as the anchor the count starts from. Clicking a vertebra moves the target; three variants can be chosen, the ordinary column of 23, a sixth lumbar (24) and a thirteenth thoracic (24), and the page shows R, C, their sum against the expected 22, a verdict (ordinary column or anomaly detected) and what the report would say: with 22 the level is reported by name, otherwise the ordinal from C2 and from the sacrum is reported and the name withheld, since a transitional column cannot be named by counting alone. It states the rule's limits: it counts and nothing more, cannot say which vertebra is extra so flags the column not the level, passes a column with both an extra and a missing vertebra, and compounds the counting error over the whole column, so one missed body anywhere flags an ordinary spine.

artifacts.question: Why count the vertebral level from the sacrum on the C-arm a hospital already owns, and what does wrong-level surgery cost?
artifacts.summary: A one-page visual abstract for spine surgeons and a hospital CFO. It frames wrong-level spine surgery as rare per operation and common per career (1 in 830 operations in a 34,544-case registry, half of surveyed surgeons), almost always a counting error under fluoroscopy, and navigation suites as too costly for a problem this rare. The method is drawn as five steps: expose at the anchor, detect bodies plus anchor (the only learned step), link overlapping frames, count k from the anchor, confirm with the instrument on bone; no tracker, no reference frame, no capital purchase. Stat tiles give operating-room time (15 to 3 minutes with a fiducial), indemnity ($75k median), navigation list price (about $1 to 2.5M, labelled an assumption) and unmeasured peace of mind, and a per-hospital model prices events and localization minutes for 300, 600 and 1,000 cases a year with every input labelled. The manuscript in preparation reports exact counts on 99.17 to 100% of reached walks with the annotation's boxes and 1,205 of 1,209 on 262 real lateral radiographs; detection is the deployment risk, which a retrospective fluoroscopy collection is asked for to measure.

key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: a 34,544-case registry puts it at 1 in 830 operations (1 in 240 in the thoracic spine), and half of surveyed spine surgeons have done it once

key_claims.claim: Most wrong-level events are intraoperative disorientation, a count that went wrong.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 81% of events are intraoperative disorientation — a count that went wrong

key_claims.claim: The method needs no tracker, reference frame or capital purchase: one learned detector and an exact count on the existing C-arm.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: no tracker, no reference frame, no capital purchase, one learned detector and an exact count

key_claims.claim: With correct boxes the count is exact on 99.17 to 100% of walks.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: with the annotation's boxes the count was exact on 99.17–100% of reached walks in twelve arms of 16 to 801 spines

key_claims.claim: On 262 real lateral radiographs from C2, 1,205 of 1,209 were counted correctly.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: on 262 real lateral radiographs from C2, 1,205 of 1,209 (99.67%)

key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Deployment risk is detection, not counting: that is what the retrospective fluoroscopy collection measures.

key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: It addresses screw placement; no published study shows it reduces wrong-level surgery.

artifacts.title: What Is Left After Physics
artifacts.readme_summary: What is left after physics, and whether a network could learn it, on four real frames
artifacts.date_evidence: No header date or stamp; the latest date mentioned is 'The 2026 diffusion paper, read directly' (Rapuri et al., arXiv:2606.21414).
artifacts.question: After a calibrated physics render of a specimen's own CT at the real C-arm pose, what residual is left in real DeepFluoro fluoroscopy frames, and could a learned CT-to-fluoroscopy model supply it?
artifacts.summary: Four real DeepFluoro frames are decomposed against renders of their own CT at the same pose (geometry checked to 0.00 px): the calibrated render alone explains 54.6 to 90.1% of attenuation variance, and a twelve-coefficient smooth field (window, scatter pedestal, heel, vignette) lifts that to 86.9 to 97.1%, so the smooth field is most of the gap. After the field the 2 to 16 px bands sit at 0.1 to 0.8% of variance, two to seven times the quantum noise floor, so the claim that a learned model would have 'nothing local' to learn was too strong; the residual is cortical edges sharper than a 1 mm CT magnified 1.5x onto 0.19 mm pixels can give, plus bowel gas that moved. The smooth field is learnable but not predictable from the CT; sharpness is only obtainable by inventing it; the bowel is unknowable. A verified literature pass (105 claims, 25 checked, 10 survived) finds the same low-frequency per-image residual in FDA, ultrasound sim-to-real, SyntheX, DeepDRR, N4 bias-field and BatchNorm work, and the 2026 diffusion paper's Table 1 shows physics DRRs with pose augmentation beating a generator at every threshold. The page ends with three direct tests to run next, read with seeds averaged and specimens as folds, because every published effect is smaller than the detector's 26-point seed spread.

key_claims.claim: The smooth per-frame field is most of the sim-to-real gap: it takes one frame from 83.0 to 91.6% explained and the worst specimen from 54.6 to 86.9%.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The smooth field takes 17-1882/000 from 83.0 to 91.6%, and 18-1109/047 from 54.6 to 86.9% — that dark right half of the frame is the device's collimation and vignette, not anatomy.

key_claims.claim: 'Nothing local' was too strong: after the field the 2 to 16 px bands are two to seven times the noise floor.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: After the field, the 2–16 px bands sit at 0.1–0.8% of the frame's variance each — two to seven times the noise floor, not at it.

key_claims.claim: The remaining edge lines come from the real frame being sharper than the CT can render; the bowel mottle is gas that moved between CT and fluoroscopy.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the CT is 1 mm voxels magnified 1.5× onto 0.19 mm pixels, and a render cannot hold detail the CT never had. The bowel mottle is gas that moved between the CT and the fluoroscopy.

key_claims.claim: A network can learn the smooth field from paired data but cannot predict it from the CT, since the device sets it per exposure.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The smooth field — yes to learn, no to predict. It is set by the device at each exposure (auto-window, exposure per view, collimation).

key_claims.claim: Cortical sharpness below CT resolution can only be invented, and no paired-DRR paper evaluated invented texture on a downstream task.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: no paired-DRR paper in the verified record evaluated that on a downstream task. For a detector this is the one place a learned term could add something, and it is also the one place it can move a label.

key_claims.claim: Fourier Domain Adaptation gains the same from an 11x11-bin band as from nine times that width, so the transferable gap lives in the smallest band.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the band can be an 11×11-bin box (β = 0.01) and the gain is the same as at nine times that width (44.6 vs 45.0 mIoU; source-only 36.6)

key_claims.claim: Ultrasound sim-to-real moved Dice 43.2 to 46.7 by swapping only DC plus the first harmonic.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the swapped band is DC plus the first harmonic — literally a per-image window/level and gradient — and it moved Dice 43.2 → 46.7

key_claims.claim: SyntheX on the same six DeepFluoro specimens reached parity with real-frame training using physics renders plus strong randomisation, and CycleGAN added nothing under strong randomisation.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: physics renders plus strong randomisation of global appearance reached parity with training on real frames (6.44 vs 6.46 mm hip landmarks)

key_claims.claim: DeepDRR's physics fidelity moved landmark error from 78.2 mm (naive) to 24.7 mm (full model); scatter moved only 26.9 to 24.7.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: naive DRRs gave 78.2 mm landmark error, polychromatic multi-material with noise 34.4, full model 24.7; scatter moved only 26.9→24.7

key_claims.claim: Removing the MRI bias field before nnU-Net gave no gain and one significant loss; under cross-vendor shift the lever was feature normalisation (InstanceNorm to BatchNorm, 0.63 to 0.80 Dice).
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: no gain on three glioma datasets and one significant loss (85 → 82 Dice; Kondrateva et al.) ... InstanceNorm→BatchNorm took cardiac Dice 0.63 → 0.80 (Full et al. 2020)

key_claims.claim: In the 2026 diffusion paper, DRRs with ±2.5° view augmentation were the best arm at every threshold; a generator wins only where the detector is already confident.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: DRRs with ±2.5° view augmentation were the best arm at every threshold (4.87 / 6.02 / 9.73). A generator wins where the detector is already confident and loses where it is not

key_claims.claim: 'Learning to project' as a deterministic map from the CT is impossible in principle, and as a learned distribution it is what randomisation already is.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: "Learning to project" as a deterministic map from the CT is impossible in principle (the field is set by the device per acquisition), and as a learned distribution it is what randomisation already is.

key_claims.claim: Every quantitative comparison cited is a single training run in its source, and every effect size is smaller than this detector's 26-point seed spread.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: every effect size in the literature (+3.5 Dice, ±0.2 mm, +0.18 Dice) is smaller than the 26-point seed spread this detector shows at one seed

artifacts.title: Ninety-Three Pixels
artifacts.readme_summary: Ninety-three pixels: DeepFluoro read to its geometry and used to calibrate the renderer against real fluoroscopy
artifacts.date_evidence: Header chip '21 Sep 2026, 03:3x EDT grid [the owner's login], branch L6_Class, 8 GPU jobs live'.
artifacts.question: Does the coarse pixel spacing of the render corpora (93 pixels for a 140 mm field) explain the detector's failures, and can the DRR renderer be calibrated against real fluoroscopy using DeepFluoro?
artifacts.summary: An overnight status board on the intraoperative level-counting work. It measures that the render corpora are 4 to 15 times coarser than a C-arm intensifier (ts_drr gives 93 px for a 140 mm field) but that a downsampling ladder on real films shows 836 px to 139 px costs 0.00 points of per-vertebra recall, so resolution is not the main event and the C2 failure needs another explanation. DeepFluoro (366 real frames, 6 cadaveric specimens, exact poses) was unblocked by presenting Chrome's TLS fingerprint, read to its geometry (reprojection 0.00 px median over 111 frames), and used to calibrate an image-formation model: physics alone explains 80.9% of attenuation variance, nine device terms add +4.3 points held out, the ceiling is 99.5%, and the residual has nothing local to learn, so the map was calibrated, not learned, and the GAN route was refuted by the literature. A two-class detector trained on 597 calibrated synthetic frames finds the sacrum on 76.9% of 365 real frames, with a 26-point seed spread bounding every arm comparison; the C2 arm's number is void (6 correct of 2593 walks) because C2 is inside a sweep frame only 15% of the time. Eight domain-randomization training arms are live, several silent failures were caught (a holdout bank deleted, films washed white, contamination checks erring toward clean), and the decision on the table is whether to re-render at C-arm resolution or price the resolution term first.

artifacts.title: Any-View Spine Plan
artifacts.readme_summary: Plan: view translation, any-position detection, paired XR-CT gold prior (patent material)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header chip 'SchwingNet · From 3D to X-ray · 21 October 2026'.
artifacts.question: Can SchwingNet turn an X-ray in one position into another view, detect and classify vertebrae at any C-arm position, and use paired X-ray and CT sets as gold truth for the 3D prior, and what must the census count before each model is trained?
artifacts.summary: A confidential (patent material, before the provisional) plan with three goals: a network that turns an X-ray in one position into another (AP to lateral), a detector and classifier that works at any position, and paired X-ray and CT sets as gold ground truth for the 3D prior. Its short answer grades them: paired X-ray and CT as gold truth is strong (registration-based labelling is near perfect in LevelCheck, 100% at 26 s, 99.3% at 7 s); any-position detection and classification is feasible with a measured gap (the project's own record on C-ArmLSpine: lateral naming 96.4% zero-shot from renders, AP naming 43.7% as a one-level counting error, detection 0.3% from renders alone, 80.5% with other devices' real frames, 84.0% with 24 frames of the device added); AP image to lateral image is hard as stated, since the closest published work (XraySyn) moves the view only 9 degrees, so the plan is structured transfer of the lateral's levels, corners and alignment from the AP, with pixel synthesis only as an auxiliary task. It tables the held paired sets (COBRA 692 cases and 375,618 projections, C-ArmLSpine 149 cases, DeepFluoro, Ljubljana, IPCAI 2025 not yet) and notes every one is lumbar or lumbosacral. Section 4 gives what the census (PR #76) must count per region with the estimated counts needed to test each approach; section 5 gives the order of work, census first, and says nothing appears in an external text before the provisional is filed.

artifacts.question: How does a new student join spine-program, set up Claude, the grid and Beethoven, and carry a first issue to a merged pull request?
artifacts.summary: An onboarding document for a student joining OpenSpineConsortium/spine-program, a private repository holding the spine imaging research as 13 numbered folders, each with its own CLAUDE.md, README.md, DATA.md, TODO.md, STATUS.md and MEMORY.md, with no imaging data in the repository. It lists the five accounts needed (GitHub write access, a Claude Pro or Max subscription at about US$20 a month, a Wayne State grid account taking about two business days, the grid's authenticator code and a Beethoven invitation), then the one-time setup of a claude.ai Project with blank instructions and of Beethoven, the Chrome extension that starts a Claude Code worker as a Slurm job in the student's grid account. Every task is one issue claimed by Claude on a branch claude/N and finished as a pull request the owner merges, with a paste-ready prompt; tasks that touch data split between the Project thread (plan, job script, pull request) and the Beethoven session (sbatch jobs), with files shipped through a clone via git archive and ssh until issue 19 settles whether the grid can reach GitHub. Issue 19 is given as the first task, with a fine-grained token kept in a mode-600 file. It closes with the rules that most often catch a new person and a table of where the long-form documents live.

artifacts.readme_summary: Steps for a student's Beethoven session to reach spine-program (Docs type, kept as Markdown)

artifacts.question: How does a student's Beethoven session on the Wayne State grid obtain a GitHub login so it can clone the private spine-program repository and push to the student's own repositories, without the token ever reaching Claude, a job script or a repository?
artifacts.summary: A four-step guide, about ten minutes each, written for a student whose Beethoven session on the Wayne State grid already clones public repositories from a compute node but lacks a login. Step 1 makes one classic personal access token with the repo scope (90-day expiry; a fine-grained token per resource owner is the fallback if the organization disallows classic tokens). Step 2 stores it in ~/.beethoven/git-credentials (mode 700 folder, 600 file) typed in an editor, points git's credential helper at it and sets the GitHub no-reply address for commits. Step 3 clones spine-program into the student's own folder on the lab volume, not under hpcworker, and checks that the clone asks for no username; it notes that results/, figures/, manuscripts/ and regulatory/ are links into a shared archive the owner has yet to fill, and points to issue 19 as a first task. Step 4 pushes to the student's own repositories, with the two-token credential.useHttpPath variant. A table of refusals (no credential file, repository not found, permission denied, invalid token, lab-volume permission, killed on the login node) closes it. Three rules frame it: the token is typed by the student alone, the Claude GitHub App links are for claude.ai sessions and are skipped, and commands run on a compute node since git is untested on the login node.

artifacts.title: State of the literature: datasets held, missing, size and power
artifacts.readme_summary: The 212-source data manifest set beside the prior research reports: which datasets are held, which are missing, their sizes and what they give the power to measure (Docs type, kept as Markdown)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Oct 8, 2026 · @[the owner]'.
artifacts.question: Which datasets of the field are held or missing, and how does the holding compare in size and statistical power with the published studies?
artifacts.summary: The 212-source manifest is cross-referenced against 114 prior research reports to say what is held by task: the large vertebra-labelled CT releases, about 20,280 transitional-screening CTs, 9,108 level-labelled real plain films, and exactly one real intraoperative human set with a volume (C-ArmLSpine). What is missing most is labelled real intraoperative frames from living patients (LevelCheck cohort, Vanderbilt, Huashan, PUMCH, SX-Stitch), all request-only with no drafted request recorded as sent, and seven gated CT collections, Merlin alone expected to add more transitional people than tier 1. Size ratios against comparable studies are larger for radiograph level identification and C-arm naming, smaller for registration, human readers, 2-D LSTV and prevalence. Every powered statement so far rests on planning accuracies of 95 to 99% that no transitional measurement supports; measured transitional figures (render L6 recall 56.1 to 72.4%, 49.9% on anomalous film windows) put every transitional test near zero power, and device-level claims cannot be tested with 4 devices. Expected transitional counts under the acquisition plan's priors are set beside calls so far, and the page lists the unknowns that change a decision and the reading it uses where two files disagree.

Approved students read everything except VinDr-SpineXR and BUU-LSPINE, held owner-only under their agreements; a table lists the decisions left to the owner and the facts no file records.

artifacts.question: Given the data the spine programme holds today, which research projects should run in what order, with what gate, n, outside check and dependency, and which unknowns still decide each one?
artifacts.summary: A research-directions page dated Oct 8, 2026, condensed from six reader notes and three independent proposals and checked by three reviewers against 711 claims, that orders the programme's work: measurement first, human reads second, models third. It finds the 2-D naming system at ceiling on ordinary spines (97.4 % of bodies on a whole lateral frame, 74.8 % with one body in view) but with zero verified real-frame transitional test persons, and argues that the published 3-D 0.990 T12-vs-L1 number is a within-patient, coronal-feature result that cannot yet serve as the parity target. It tables every mechanism tried on transitional spines with its measured result, the fluoroscopy, paired, CT and unused data sources with their restrictions, the pre-stated gates against today's n, and eleven CT projects with their gates and outside checks. It lays out a three-stage visibility experiment (single-vertebra 3-D target on the laptop, projected morphometry at exact pose on the 802 v11 volumes, then real frames) with ICC and AUC gates, five model variants held until stage 2 reports, and a ranked list of sixteen projects with a week-one order in which no model trains. It closes with where the three proposals disagreed and a table of the unknowns that decide each project and where each was looked for.

decisions.decision: The standing determination: name the level correctly on a transitional spine (L6, T13, sacralised L5, four lumbar) from C-arm exposures at parity with an ordinary spine, and report "not at parity" plainly if that is the result.
decisions.reason: Narrower and stronger than "anomaly-aware"; Castellvi type I is unrecoverable from a lateral by construction, so the target is the count-changing types II to IV.

decisions.decision: The page takes proposal B as the programme, grafting A's smallest-experiment-that-changes-a-decision rule and its ordering of the ratio-only run first, and C's venue and power discipline.
decisions.reason: The three asks are B's structure and its feature-level specification is what a student can act on.

decisions.decision: The 85 % bound on the 43 test L6 persons allows one miss, not two.
decisions.reason: 42 of 43 gives 87.9 %, 41 of 43 gives 84.5 %.

decisions.decision: Mixed training (renders and real films in every batch) is the default schedule.
decisions.reason: Pretrain-then-fine-tune lost 25.6 anomalous points.

decisions.decision: The clean encoder starts from ImageNet on G3 training persons only, with no decoder pseudolabels and FluoroCap in no training list.
decisions.reason: 92 of 97 transitional validation and test persons sit in the v8 and v9 training splits.

decisions.decision: Excluded by the record: Star Temporal Classification, CycleGAN, ADDA, CUT and SDXL restyling, decoder-named pseudolabels, size in millimetres as a scalar, and a learned refiner as the 2-D reference.
decisions.reason: Each returned no gain or was refuted in measured arms.

decisions.decision: Stop rule for FLU-2: zero or one miss of the 7 render-scoreable validation L6 persons proceeds to three seeds and two heads; two or more misses stops the fluoroscopy arm and the manuscript says "not at parity" with the number.
decisions.reason: At a true recall of 72.4 % the screen passes 38 % of the time, at 85 % 72 %.

decisions.decision: No G3 test person is scored until paper 2's ledger carries an "H1 seen" entry; if the read confirms fewer than 22 carriers with an exported frame, no fluoroscopy transitional sensitivity is claimed and the render number is reported alone.
decisions.reason: The data requests are the only route to 22.

decisions.decision: No weight trained with BUU laterals leaves until the owner has read the licence.
decisions.reason: The BUU EULA forbids redistribution and the licence reading for derived labels is open.

decisions.decision: Each model variant V0 to V4 is built only after stage 2 has said which features a view carries and after the owner's decision.
decisions.reason: None starts until the visibility experiment has reported.

decisions.decision: Pooled device numbers are never quoted without the device-held-out arm beside them; the published 0.990 is reported as the ceiling, never as the 3-D side of parity.
decisions.reason: Each C-arm is its own domain; the 0.990 is a within-patient number.

decisions.decision: Before a student copy is made, the sentences naming the technology-transfer office and the proposal judging are cut.
decisions.reason: The rest is written to be student-safe.

decisions.decision: CT-11 (prone and supine segmental mobility) is recorded as a later paper, not a now-thing.
If the re-reads move a record, the G3 split changes and the leak audit is re-run before FLU-2 scores anyone; nothing trains on the flagship recipe before gates G0 to G3 close.
decisions.reason: The pipeline-state tool on the grid is the authority on which gates are closed.

artifacts.summary: The shareable summary of the handoff written into spinesurg-ct-nnunet/HANDOFF/ on 8 October 2026. It names the one question (naming a vertebral level from what the surgeon has in the room, without counting from C2 or a registered scan), the four projects and where each lives, and the five pieces of the SchwingNet model with what each trained on: a YOLO11m-pose body detector on 12,709 films, a YOLO11m vertebra and sacrum detector on 3,094 real frames, the allspine_v9 ResNet-18 level encoder with 27 classes, a BiGRU recurrent head, and five C-ArmLSpine fold models. It flags a defect to decide on (the fold banks still hold VinDr and FluoroCap crops against the directive), that real C-arm data is barely used, and the results catalog's headline numbers (97.4% of bodies named on a whole lateral frame, 97.0% from the count alone, 80.5% held-out-device recall, a comparator at 97.6% that cannot be exceeded). It lists the regeneration recipes, the manuscripts and their states (paper 1 held pending technology transfer, NeurIPS 3474 accepted as a poster, CNS 2026 accepted), the hold-out rule of 2026-09-23 with checks CHK-1 to CHK-9, the two historical leaks (NHANES II twice, CTSpinoPelvic1K twice) that make allspine v2, v6, v7, anchor_drr and vindrps record only, the ten rules, a student's first week, and what context was exported. The results catalog wins over any other file or memory note.

artifacts.title: Vertebra Detector Field Report
artifacts.readme_summary: Field report on a vertebra detector (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: No header date, run stamp or 'as of' line; the only years named are the NHANES II film years ('NHANES II film, 1976–80'), which date the dataset, not the artifact.
artifacts.question: How well does a single-class vertebra detector, trained on a union of partially-labelled public spine-radiograph datasets, locate every vertebral body and its four corners when measured per source rather than pooled?
artifacts.summary: A stage-1 field report on a class-agnostic vertebra detector (YOLO11m-pose, one class, four corner keypoints, 1024 px, 111 epochs on one H200) trained on three credential-free sources (NHANES II film, Mendeley 716 standing DR, a partial BUU-LSPINE download): 958 images, 6073 instances, 727 patients with patient-disjoint splits. It reports box mAP@50 0.980 and corner mAP@50 0.922 on validation, AP@50 0.957 and PCK@0.2 91.7% on a 558-instance held-out test, and 6.8 ms inference per image, broken out per source and per acquisition. The single-class design is justified by the confounding of level identity with dataset of origin; level naming is deferred to a second head not yet started. The page states plainly that the ignore-region loss mask is written but not wired in, that every test image comes from a source the model trained on, that no cross-site or intraoperative data is present, and that VinDr-SpineXR, IEEE DataPort, CSXA, the full BUU, CM Spine and AASCE are blocked on credentials or transfer limits. Two parsing bugs caught by validators (BUU step-2 edge pairing, Roboflow duplicate hashes) are recorded, and the reproduce commands are given.

key_claims.claim: The detector reaches box mAP@50 0.980 and corner mAP@50 0.922 on validation, AP@50 0.957 and PCK@0.2 91.7% on the held-out test, at 6.8 ms per image.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 0.980 Box mAP@50 · val / 0.922 Corner mAP@50 · val / 0.957 AP@50 · held-out test / 91.7% PCK@0.2 · test / 6.8 ms Inference / image

key_claims.claim: Training per-level classes on a union of partially-labelled datasets confounds level identity with dataset of origin, so the detector carries one class and leaves level to a later head.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: a class that appears in exactly one source can be predicted from scanner style rather than anatomy. So the detector carries one class.

key_claims.claim: The headline numbers are in-distribution: the ignore-region loss mask is written but the trained model used cropping only, and the union-with-ignore ablation has not been run.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The ignore-region loss mask is written ( src/ignore.py ) but the trained model below used cropping only. The headline numbers are therefore in-distribution

key_claims.claim: Every test image comes from a source the model also trained on; nothing is cross-site.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: None of these are cross-site. Every test image comes from a source the model also trained on.

key_claims.claim: Corner mAP@50-95 reaches 0.901, which the report values over the box number because it says the corners land tightly.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: corner mAP@50-95 reaches 0.901 , which matters more than the box number

key_claims.claim: Two parsing bugs were caught by validators: BUU edge lines pair step-2 rather than consecutively, and Roboflow exports duplicated 107 instances across splits.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: BUU's edge lines pair step-2, not consecutively ... Roboflow exports the same image into train/valid/test under different hashes, which duplicated 107 instances

key_claims.claim: Horizontal flip is disabled because on a lateral radiograph it swaps the anterior/posterior meaning of the corner slots and the keypoint head fails to converge.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Horizontal flip is disabled : on a lateral radiograph a flip is anatomically impossible and silently swaps the anterior/posterior meaning of the corner slots

key_claims.claim: The 0.861 (BUU) versus 0.970 (NHANES) gap is not yet a measurement because BUU contributes only 15 test instances.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: BUU contributes only 15 test instances here, so that gap is not yet a measurement.

key_claims.claim: Recall is not reported globally because on partially-labelled sources a missed vertebra may be one the dataset never annotated; detections are scored only inside the trusted-background region.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Recall is not reported globally, by design. On partially-labelled sources a “missed” vertebra may be one the dataset never annotated.

key_claims.claim: The intended external hold-outs (VinDr-SpineXR, IEEE DataPort's 236 films) are blocked on credentials, so no genuinely external test set exists yet.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Blocked on credentials, not on work. ... until they exist there is no genuinely external test set.

key_claims.claim: CSXA's 4,963 images are behind a SciDB browser session and four candidate API endpoints all returned errors; its absence is the biggest gap in the corpus.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the 4,963 images sit behind a SciDB browser session; four candidate API endpoints all returned errors.

key_claims.claim: The 0.957 AP@50 demonstrates the pipeline is correct end to end but is not evidence of cross-site generalization.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: It demonstrates the pipeline is correct end to end. It is not evidence of cross-site generalization, which is the property the project exists to establish.

artifacts.title: Naming Vertebrae Without an Anchor
artifacts.readme_summary: Naming vertebrae with no anchor, with 12 figures (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Byline under the title: "Detroit Medical Center / Wayne State University · September 17, 2026"; the page also carries a "Latest · ... what is running tonight" section with live job ids.
artifacts.question: Can a registration-free classifier name vertebral levels on a limited-field radiograph that holds no anatomic anchor, and does a short sweep of overlapping exposures recover what a single exposure cannot?
artifacts.summary: A research page, styled as a manuscript in preparation for Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, that tests a feasibility report's claim that level naming in the anchor-free isolated stack (its State C) is mathematically underdetermined. A ResNet-18 crop encoder with a bidirectional GRU head over 2-9 vertebrae, trained on banks v2 through v6 of CT renders and real films, named ordinary spines at 97.2% and anomalous spines at 87.2% in the label-defined isolated stack on real film, and 91.8% ordinary versus 66.0% anomalous on interior windows whose pixels hold neither end of the stack, against a 0% placement-blind baseline. The predicted failure mechanism is real but bounded (83% of errors are one-level shifts) and the report's geometric substitutes did not transfer to real film (the normal-L5 Wigh band held 5.1% of ordinary films). A sweep of overlapping C-arm frames linked from a landmark and decoded as one chain raised two-vertebra frames from 69.6% to 95.1% and thoracic frames from 13.4% to 97.1-99.3% on renders, with two bodies of overlap as the optimum. The page records its retractions (an earlier decoder claim was a tautology of the code; the 20-film 87% was six points optimistic, v6 gives 81.3% on 4,026 windows and 49.9% on anomalous interior windows), its weak spots (L6 under 50%, never seen on a photograph), the data-quality interventions, every network tested, a prior-art table and the reproduction commands.

key_claims.claim: The anchor-free isolated stack is not underdetermined: on real film it carries level information with a measured, anomaly-dependent cost.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The isolated stack is not underdetermined; it carries information the report said could not exist, with a measured, anomaly-dependent cost

key_claims.claim: On interior windows whose pixels exclude both ends of the stack, ordinary lumbar naming is 91.8% against a 0% placement-blind baseline.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: ordinary lumbar naming was 91.8% [89.4, 94.1] (455 films) and anomalous 66.0% [39.6, 87.2] (12 films), against a placement-blind baseline of 0%

key_claims.claim: The predicted failure mechanism (an integer offset between five- and six-lumbar readings) is real but bounded: most errors are one-level shifts.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 83.0% of isolated-stack errors are exactly one level (52% too low, 31% too high); 44.9% of errored windows carry one coherent offset

key_claims.claim: L6 is named correctly less than half the time because the model has never seen a photograph of a six-lumbar spine; it is a data problem, not a loss-function problem.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: That is the whole explanation of the 57–80% L6 figure, and it is a data problem, not a loss-function problem

key_claims.claim: The report's geometric detectors do not transfer to real film; only sacral slope separates six-lumbar spines.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the stated normal-L5 squaring band held 5.1% of ordinary films; only sacral slope separated six-lumbar spines (AUC 0.73)

key_claims.claim: A sweep of overlapping frames from a landmark, linked into one chain, recovers the single-exposure limitation without a preoperative CT.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: raised two-vertebra frames from 69.6% to 95.1% and, through the thoracic spine, from 13.4% to 97.1%; three-vertebra frames there reached 99.3%

key_claims.claim: Two bodies of overlap between exposures is the optimum; the protocol, not the network, buys the last four points.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Two is the optimum: below it the linker is working from partial bodies at the seam; above it the extra exposures add links faster than they add evidence

key_claims.claim: Decoding the chain as one sequence against four alphabets with the landmark declared is the lever, worth 9.7 points on identical features.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: names 95.5% — 9.7 points from the decoding step alone, on identical features

key_claims.claim: Training on 76,042 decoder-pseudolabelled crops (bank v5) cut anomalous accuracy while leaving ordinary accuracy unchanged.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: training on 76,042 pseudolabelled crops cut anomalous accuracy to 66.8% while leaving ordinary accuracy unchanged

key_claims.claim: The 20-film 87% figure was optimistic; v6, with all 144 anomalous BUU studies in the test partition, gives 81.3%, and on interior windows an anomalous body is named at a coin toss.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: exact naming is 81.3% [80.0, 82.4] (cross-entropy) ... with the junction out of the picture an anomalous body is named at a coin toss between its two candidate identities

key_claims.claim: The earlier claim that the decoder chose a variant template only on films not reaching the junction was a tautology of the page's own code and is retracted.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: That was a tautology of our own code: the pseudolabelling script clears the supervision tier at and below the junction whenever it flags a variant

key_claims.claim: No published method chains consecutive frames from a landmark to name what lies between them.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A verified search found no published method that chains consecutive frames from a landmark to name what lies between them

key_claims.claim: Several of the feasibility report's own citations do not exist or are misdefined.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: none of the seven numbers appears in any indexed paper; the literature's discriminant is a length threshold

key_claims.claim: Six interventions aimed at the transitional number; only the sweep moved it.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Six interventions aimed at the transitional number; only the sweep moved it.

key_claims.claim: A decline is not a free retake: frames shot again from a quarter-vertebra away score the same.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The retakes score the same as the frames they replaced — 81.3% against 82.8% at 82% coverage

key_claims.claim: Lumbosacral and thoracolumbar anomalies co-occur, by less than first tabulated.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On the 280 subjects with both ends graded: OR 3.61, exact 95% CI [2.08, 6.27]

key_claims.claim: The real-film vertebra detector does not transfer to degraded CT renders, so the render arms measure the linker and decoder, not the whole pipeline.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: with its boxes the chain came out complete on 0.4% of spines. The render arms therefore measure the linker and the decoder, not the whole pipeline.

key_claims.claim: Level identity is redundant and distributed across the body, end-plates and neighbours; no single region is load-bearing and no ratio of two lengths is what the encoder reads.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Identity is redundant and distributed; no ratio of two lengths is what the encoder reads — which is why the geometric indices failed on real film

decisions.decision: v6 moves all 144 anomalous BUU studies to the test partition, duplicates anomalous CT renders x4 in training and changes nothing else, so the ordinary column is a control.
decisions.reason: 124 of the 144 wrongly counted studies sat in the training partition of every bank so far, so the 87% was measured on a model trained to give the ordinary answer on siblings of its test films

decisions.decision: v6 changes the labels, not the architecture.
decisions.reason: every ResNet-18 arm sits within 0.6 points and nothing tested beats the recipe

decisions.decision: All 144 BUU anomalous studies barred from training; the S1a line promoted to an L6 box on six-lumbar studies and L5 flagged sacralised on four-lumbar.
decisions.reason: BUU's counted names are wrong on those studies by the dataset's own reading

decisions.decision: A film with no anomaly ground truth is dropped from the split rather than assumed ordinary.
decisions.reason: reading absence of evidence as absence of anomaly manufactures specificity

decisions.decision: The pooled cross-cohort odds ratio is not reported.
decisions.reason: VerSe base rates are not prevalences and the pooled figure is Simpson's paradox

decisions.decision: The earlier claim that the decoder chose a variant template only on films not reaching the junction (D2) is retracted and replaced.
decisions.reason: it was a tautology of the page's own pseudolabelling code

decisions.decision: The bank builder refuses unfitted film-noise parameters; a guessed setting was discarded.
decisions.reason: the guessed setting overshot (noise 0.049, SNR 20); the fitted knobs land inside the real films' band

decisions.decision: The film-look diffusion filter is trained on the public digitised X-ray datasets only, with FluoroCap excluded by an assertion that aborts the build.
Renders whose vertebrae flip the encoder's answer on more than 20% of bodies are dropped.
The sweep protocol asks for four vertebrae in the frame.
decisions.reason: two vertebrae on a thoracolumbar-variant spine scores 50% at T11-T12; four fixes it

decisions.decision: A decline means count, or sweep further, not move and reshoot.
decisions.reason: retakes from a quarter-vertebra away score the same as the frames they replaced

decisions.decision: The operating configuration for every sweep arm is a 9-inch intensifier field, two bodies of overlap, sweeping up from the sacrum.
decisions.reason: two bodies is the measured optimum; it matches the only clinical stitching series' four to six exposures with 20-30% overlap

decisions.decision: Two discarded runs (a head paired with the wrong encoder; two separability runs that fell back to one cohort) are recorded rather than hidden.
When the real-film sweep arms land they replace the render table rather than sit beside it.
decisions.reason: the current per-level table is on CT scans rendered as radiographs

decisions.decision: Transitional-cell intervals are printed rather than smoothed.
decisions.reason: denominators are 9 to 45 vertebrae per cell

artifacts.notes: The page is the fullest statement of the SchwingNet method in this batch: crop scale, the GRU head, the four-alphabet sequence decode, the sweep protocol's linker restricted to the asked-for step, the pseudolabel gating rule and the film-noise model. It is explicit about its own corrections (the D2 retraction, the v6 re-partition) and about what is measured on renders versus real film. The author is named in the byline; recorded here by role.

artifacts.date_evidence: Header line: "transitional-term figures: PubMed Central pass one, plus OpenAlex and preprint PDFs, Open-i, MedPix and Wikimedia Commons · 15 September 2026".
artifacts.question: Which of the gathered transitional-term figures are usable human X-ray or fluoroscopy images, what lumbosacral or thoracolumbar transitional finding is actually visible in each, and does the caption's numbering need a note?
artifacts.summary: A reviewer's bench page over figures gathered on 15 September 2026 from PubMed Central (pass one), OpenAlex and preprint PDFs, Open-i, MedPix and Wikimedia Commons by transitional-vertebra search terms; the data file holds 585 rows, each with source id, caption, journal, year, licence, size, a modality guess, a family tag, caption-derived levels and L6/T13 flags, and a thumbnail. For each figure the reviewer marks what it is (human radiograph, fluoroscopy/C-arm, CT scout, CT or MRI, not an X-ray, animal), which finding is visible (L6, sacralized L5 by Castellvi, lumbarized S1, T13 or 13th rib, lumbar rib at L1, absent or hypoplastic 12th rib, cervical rib, wrong-level montage, none, unsure), a quality verdict (usable, too small, composite needing splitting) and a free numbering note. Verdicts save to the page's store as they are clicked, with keyboard shortcuts 1 to 6 for type and j/k to move; only figures with a saved type count as reviewed, and the counters (reviewed, usable human X-ray/fluoro, with a transitional finding) are filled at runtime, showing 0 of 0 in the static text.
