artifacts.title: FluoroCap Corpus Audit
artifacts.readme_summary: Audit of the FluoroCap corpus (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Corpus audit · 14 September 2026' and the footer 'Generated from tools/fluorocap_qc.py against the decode of 14 September 2026.'
artifacts.question: What does the mined FluoroCap corpus hold, what are its machine-assigned vertebra pseudolabels worth when the caption is held out, and what blocks a morphology-based vertebra detector?
artifacts.summary: An audit of eleven thousand spine radiograph panels mined from journal figures and surgical video, of which about three thousand carry machine-assigned vertebra labels. It finds that image size is the binding constraint (half the corpus is smaller than the level classifier's 320-pixel crop window), that the transitional classes T13 and L6 have never been assigned to any real panel, and that caption-held-out containment is 56.8% on 389 panels while the level model alone is right 38.3% of the time. A cross-check through one code path shows the level model scoring 98.7% on its own validation split but 35.7% on CT renders, traced to a training bank built from cervical and lumbar films with zero thoracic crops, so re-weighting cannot help. Constraint decoding lifts caption-free same-figure region agreement from 52.1% to 91.5%, and single-crop morphology holds from L1 to L4 on six-lumbar spines but never recognises the L6 itself. No panel has been read by a human, so every accuracy figure is agreement between automatic sources; the page ends with an ordered list: read 400 panels, finish the all-spine bank and retrain, oversample T13 and L6, raise resolution, fold in the self-trained detector.

key_claims.claim: Only 29% of known panels produced a vertebra box, and much of the missing 71% is detector miss rather than non-radiograph panels, since the modality classifier scores 93% held out.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Only 29% of known panels produced a vertebra box . The modality classifier scores 93% on a held-out set of 2,143 panels, so a large share of the missing 71% is detector miss

key_claims.claim: Image size, not contrast or sharpness, is the binding constraint: half the corpus is smaller than the classifier's 320-pixel crop window.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 45.8% of panels fall below 224 pixels and only 7.9% reach 512.

key_claims.claim: T13 and L6 have never been assigned to a single real panel, so the transitional-anatomy claim has no real-image evidence behind it.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: T13 and L6 have never been assigned to a single real panel. Both are in the model's 27-class output

key_claims.claim: Caption-held-out containment is 56.8% (n = 389) and only that row is a test; rows where the caption constrained the search agree 100% and prove nothing.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Where it did, agreeing with the caption afterwards proves nothing. The corpus splits cleanly on that flag, and only the second row below is a test.

key_claims.claim: The level model alone is right 38.3% of the time on caption-held-out panels; every outside evidence term beats it, so the corpus must not be used to retrain the level model without re-weighting.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The level model alone is right 38.3% of the time on panels where the caption was held back.

key_claims.claim: The collapse outside the lumbar spine is absence of training data, not imbalance: the bank holds no thoracic films and T2 through T11, T13 and L6 have zero training crops, so re-weighting would do nothing.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: T2 through T11, T13 and L6 have exactly zero training crops; T12, the sacrum, C1, C2 and T1 have between 22 and 190.

key_claims.claim: The model scores 98.7% on its own validation split but 35.7% on CT renders through the same code path.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 98.7% own validation split, one crop at a time ... 35.7% CT renders, same code path

key_claims.claim: At L1 the gap between own films (85.4%) and renders (43.0%) is domain, not coverage.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: That difference is domain, not coverage, and it is what the cone-beam renderer and a resolution-degradation augmentation are for.

key_claims.claim: Constraint decoding recovers structure the classifier lacks: caption-free same-figure region agreement rises from 52.1% to 91.5%.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Constraint decoding lifts caption-free region agreement from 52.1% to 91.5% and the rate of substantially overlapping level sets from 30.8% to 68.2%.

key_claims.claim: Single-crop morphology holds from L1 to L4 on six-lumbar spines but the L6 is never recognised and L5 collapses, which is the safety case for the rare classes.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On a six-lumbar spine this classifier would confidently call the sixth lumbar vertebra an L5.

key_claims.claim: No panel has been read by a human; every accuracy figure is agreement between two automatic sources and bounds error from one side only.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: No panel in this corpus has been read by a human. Every accuracy figure above is agreement between two automatic sources

key_claims.claim: Hardware robustness is not a measured property: the zero-shot implant detector has 33% recall and no labelled implant set exists on real panels.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The zero-shot implant detector was hand-checked at 33% recall with 28% false positives.

key_claims.claim: The CT render banks show the mechanism: roughly 1,100 examples of each lumbar level against 68 L6 and 6 T13, a ratio no re-weighting rescues.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: No re-weighting will rescue a 180-to-1 ratio; the render banks have to change.

artifacts.title: Vertebral Levels Without CT
artifacts.readme_summary: Level identification without CT (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Dateline under the lead: "18 September 2026 · every figure measured on held-out data"; the page also says a literature search "finished today".
artifacts.question: Can vertebrae be named from C-arm spot films without a CT by matching them onto a map built from a short sweep of overlapping exposures, and what still stands between that and a clinical result?
artifacts.summary: An internal summary of a level-identification method that never counts: a short sweep of overlapping fluoroscopic exposures from a landmark (the sacrum or C2) builds a map of the patient's own spine, and later spot films are matched onto it. On twelve held-out whole-spine studies a thoracic two-vertebra film is named 4.3% alone and 91.3% matched (three vertebrae: 22.2% to 96.3%); lumbar real films go from 78.7% to 93.6%; per vertebra T11 to L5 the matched accuracy is 91.7 to 96.8%. All figures were re-measured after an audit found the earlier evaluation overlapped the training set, which had inflated the baseline rather than the sweep. Two bodies of overlap is the working point (3.0 exposures, 98.3%). Two things do not work yet: the automatic vertebra finder's duplicated boxes (17.9%), traced to a linking rule, made the sweep worse than not sweeping; and transitional spines are unmeasured with eight held-out cases. The page sets the literature straight (LevelCheck's 99.998% is a convergence rate; the only comparable figure is 88.3% on cadaveric long films), adopts a disc-based rule for sacral fusion, shows that lowering the detector threshold is the wrong lever, and asks the group to work three Hugging Face review sites (plain radiographs, published figures, a surgeon reader study) before a retrospective collection at DMC and a prospective study. Marked not for distribution outside the group.

decisions.decision: Adopt the rule: look for the disc, not the fusion. A body still separated from the sacrum by a disc is a separate vertebra and counts; if the disc is gone it is part of the sacrum; a disc between S1 and S2 makes the top segment separate.
decisions.reason: Every major dataset avoids the case, surgeons agree only a third of the time on the sacral endplate, and the disc is the one thing visible and decidable.

decisions.decision: Keep two bodies of overlap between exposures as the working point.
decisions.reason: Past two bodies the sweep needs more than twice the exposures and loses accuracy; the point survived the re-measurement.

decisions.decision: Keep the detector threshold at 0.25; lowering it is ruled out as the wrong lever.
decisions.reason: Misses stay at 2.4% at every setting while spurious boxes double and the map survives on 8% instead of 40% of films.

decisions.decision: Give the sacrum a detector of its own and define its target as the S1 body between its endplates; a partially lumbarised S1 gets its own box.
decisions.reason: Two of the three remaining misses are the sacrum, and losing it costs the anchor the whole map is built from.

decisions.decision: No figure will be quoted for transitional spines from the eight held-out cases, and no rate from the reader study.
decisions.reason: Eight spines cannot distinguish 60% from 95%; the ten transitional misnamed frames are a census, not a sample.

decisions.decision: Annotation order: finish the plain radiographs first, then the published figures; a twelve-case quiz (nine needed) gates entry and is taken once.
decisions.reason: The first set is easier to learn on; shared misconceptions between readers would be written into the training set.

decisions.decision: The reader study shows a deliberately wrong suggestion on 33 of 77 films and cuts each film's travel short of the sacrum.
decisions.reason: To measure how often a confident wrong suggestion talks a correct reader out of a correct answer.

decisions.decision: Solve the detector problem before the C-arm packaging question.
decisions.reason: No use putting a system on a C-arm while automatic vertebra-finding makes it worse than doing nothing.

decisions.decision: Everything is re-measured with the training exclusion enforced by the tool, replacing the earlier version of the page.
decisions.reason: An audit found the evaluation and training set overlapped through a patient-grouped split the evaluation scripts could not see.

decisions.decision: Not for distribution outside the group.

artifacts.coverage_notes: The HTML page's bar charts were extracted as text, so axis tick labels (0-100%, 80-100%) appear as stray lines; the figures' values were read from the labels and recorded. The folder holds only index.html; no image file. The third review site's address carries an account name resembling a person's; it is recorded as an address only. No instruction-like text was found. Internal inconsistency: the lumbar real-film n is 25 films in the stat tile and n=24 in the chart. 70 numbers recorded; the per-threshold and per-overlap table rows were folded into one entry each.
artifacts.notes: The page describes method detail (sweep and match, the linking rule, detector thresholds, the sacrum as anchor, the disc rule for fusion) and also the annotation and reader-study programme and the clinical path, hence mixed. It explicitly supersedes an earlier version of itself whose numbers were inflated by a train/test leak. The quoted 97.6% LevelCheck figure is framed as a team (human-plus-machine) score, not a comparator for the machine alone.

artifacts.question: Which of nine public spine radiograph sources did the spine-detector pipeline actually obtain, why did the rest fail to download, and how does the collaborator taking the handoff get each one, ordered by how fast it unblocks?
artifacts.summary: A handoff for the spine-detector pipeline's collaborator covering nine public spine radiograph sources. The manifest holds 6,073 vertebra instances from three ingested sources (NHANES II annotated subset, Mendeley 716 spondylolisthesis, and 77 BUU-LSPINE files), of which only 125 are AP against 5,948 lateral, so AP is the gap. The two biggest wins need no permission: a 400-pair BUU-LSPINE subset already sits on the owner's PC un-ingested, and the 2,000-pair subset is a single Google Drive zip that sidesteps the gdown folder cap that stopped the first download at 77 files. It corrects an earlier report: VinDr-SpineXR is PhysioNet restricted-access (register, sign the DUA, same day), not credentialed. CSXA (4,963 annotated cervical laterals) has zero images on disk only because Science Data Bank's download is a JavaScript UI behind a login; CM Spine's Drive link refused gdown; the BUU full release, AASCE/SpineWeb Dataset 16 and the IEEE DataPort lateral set need forms or a subscription. It closes with rules: everything lands on the grid, patient-disjoint splits, never invent levels, three sources not to use, and acknowledge every source.

artifacts.title: FluoroCap Reality Check
artifacts.readme_summary: FluoroCap reality check (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'FluoroCap · validation · 15 September 2026'; 'All counts are snapshots from 15 Sep 2026, roughly 06:55-07:15 grid time'; 'Fifteen agents in one run on 15 September 2026, 06:55 to 07:35 grid time'.
artifacts.question: Can the FluoroCap corpus and the level model, as they exist on 15 September 2026, support a 99% level-identification claim on real fluoroscopy, and what would it take to get there?
artifacts.summary: A validation page dated 15 September 2026 that measures what the FluoroCap corpus and the level model actually prove, ranks the blockers to a 99% claim by the strength of the evidence, condenses six literature sweeps (datasets, methods, synthetic-to-real, edge cases, acquisition, resolution) and lays out a from-scratch target, data plan, edge-case coverage table, evaluation protocol and 90-day and 12-month schedule. It finds exactly one held-out number (98.7% exact on 8,422 radiograph crops with human labels), no human-verified fluoroscopy panel (0 of 17,486 manifest rows), every render figure overlapping training, no real image with an L6 or T13 label, the level model as the weakest decoder term (37.9% on 169 real panels) and the v2 weights destroyed. The literature holds no synthetic-trained classifier reaching 95-99% on real fluoroscopy, discrete labels lose 9-28 points at the domain boundary, and the one real-film LSTV classifier reaches 76.4%. The verdict is that the approach is sound as a research direction and unmeasured as a claim, and that the binding constraint is labelled real intraoperative images, not pixels; the plan's Tier 0 is a registration-labelled PACS pull plus raw 3D C-arm projections, with the mined figures kept as an external test set only. The page was produced by fifteen agents in 41 minutes, with 48 literature claims checked against their sources (36 confirmed, 12 corrected, none refuted).

key_claims.claim: The thesis that local shape identifies a vertebral level is sound as a research direction but unmeasured as a claim.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: So the approach is sound as a research direction and unmeasured as a claim.

key_claims.claim: The only held-out accuracy the files prove is 98.7% single-crop on 8,422 cervical and lumbar radiograph crops with human labels; nothing applies to fluoroscopy.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: one number, 98.7% single-crop on 8,422 held-out cervical and lumbar radiograph crops at 0.17 mm/px with human labels, and nothing else

key_claims.claim: No real image in the corpus carries a human-verified level; every manifest row is caption-derived with readers pending.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Every one of the 17,486 manifest rows reads "caption-derived (author-stated level); reader labels pending"; qc_report.json records adjudicated_gold_panels 0

key_claims.claim: Every render evaluation overlaps training, so no honest render number and no learning curve exist.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The 92.7% diag is on training cases; L6 100% is 13 training crops; sacrum is 100% on renders and 11.9% caption-free on real panels

key_claims.claim: The level model alone is the weakest decider on real panels.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the level model alone is the weakest term in the decoder on real panels (37.9% on 169)

key_claims.claim: The all-spine v2 model exists only as a validation JSON; its weights were destroyed by the chain's link step and a retrain was pending.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: weights destroyed by the chain's link step; retrain 40285209 pending at read time

key_claims.claim: The literature contains no synthetic-trained classifier reaching 95-99% on real fluoroscopy; discrete-label precedents drop 9-28 points at the domain boundary.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The literature contains no synthetic-trained classifier that reaches 95-99% on real fluoroscopy; the classification-shaped precedents drop 9-28 points at the domain boundary

key_claims.claim: Caption labels carry 5-10% counting-convention noise concentrated in the transitional stratum, making a 99% target against them uninterpretable.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A 99% target measured against labels wrong in one case in twelve is uninterpretable, and the error concentrates in exactly the transitional stratum the project exists for.

key_claims.claim: Transitional anatomy has no real positive and thin synthetic support, which caps accuracy at about 94% before any other error.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: roughly one patient in ten has a count the caption or the counter gets wrong; at 46% on those the ceiling is about 94% before any other error

key_claims.claim: Hardware supervision is entirely synthetic while 57% of the included test panels are instrumented.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Hardware supervision is entirely synthetic while the test set is 57% instrumented.

key_claims.claim: The thoracic spine has zero real training images and is the highest-risk region; an overall 99% would hide a thoracic figure below 60.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The v2 bank holds no real-film crops at T2-T11 (T1 56, T12 382); v1 scores 43-58% on normal renders at T3-T9

key_claims.claim: The mined figures are a test set, not a training set: captions, burned-in text, compound-figure noise and duplicates make them unfit for level training.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Training a level head on this teaches arrows and captions; evaluating on it requires reading.

key_claims.claim: The median panel gives about 0.55 mm per pixel and a 55-px lumbar vertebra, 2.6x coarser than the DRRs the model trains on; upsampling adds no edges and super-resolution is not a fix.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The model upsamples 1.75× at the median and 4.6× at p10 to reach its 96-px target, which adds no edges, and the DRRs it trains on are 2.6× sharper per vertebra

key_claims.claim: The binding constraint is labelled real intraoperative images, not pixels, and the mined figures cannot supply them.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Data is the problem, but the binding constraint is labelled real intraoperative images, not pixels, and the mined figures cannot supply them

key_claims.claim: The modality classifier finds 49% of the released panels not an x-ray at all, and 35% of level-labelled decoded panels not a spine radiograph.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 8,843 (49%) score as not an x-ray at all ... Of the 2,071 decoded panels that carry level labels, 732 (35%) are panels the classifier calls not a spine radiograph

key_claims.claim: The CUT translator's 'real fluoroscopy' target was the unfiltered panel directories (an axial MRI, a lightbox photo, a screenshot), so the v1 translation result is not a test of translation.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Its "real fluoroscopy" domain was the panel directories as they are, so the v1 translation result is not a test of translation.

key_claims.claim: A 99% claim requires the lower interval bound above 98% in every primary stratum, about 1,500 verified vertebrae per stratum.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A 99% claim requires the lower interval bound above 98% in every primary stratum, which means about 1,500 verified vertebrae per stratum.

key_claims.claim: CT-to-image registration (LevelCheck) is the only method with 100% on real intraoperative images, and the best CT-free learned result on a real intraoperative modality is 88.3% on uninstrumented cadavers.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the bar for a CT-free method on a real intraoperative modality is 88% on uninstrumented cadavers ... 99% has no precedent from any direction

key_claims.claim: Physics fidelity of renders matters more than volume at the start, and dense geometric tasks transfer while discrete labels do not.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Physics matters more than volume at the start ... Dense geometric tasks transfer ... Discrete labels do not transfer

decisions.decision: Recommended: stop training or fine-tuning any level head on caption-derived labels, and keep the mined figures and video (Tier 4) as an external test set only, after a two-reader read of a stratified sample.
decisions.reason: Their labels are captions, two-thirds carry burned-in text and 3.6% a printed level label, which a network will learn; training on them teaches arrows and captions.

decisions.decision: Recommended: stop quoting render accuracy without a split filter, and add one to diag_level_model.py and eval_transitional.py.
decisions.reason: Every render evaluation overlaps training; the 92.7% diag is on training cases and L6 100% is 13 training crops.

decisions.decision: Recommended: stop scaling the YouTube and Instagram harvests, counting label tokens as images, carrying NHANES twice in the bank as nhanes_drr, duplicating L6 crops, and treating figure-mate agreement or caption-free containment as accuracy.
decisions.reason: The harvests turned 541,621 frame records into 1,462 panels capped at 720p and 1,633 unlabelled images; 12x L6 duplication did not move L6; agreement measures are model-versus-model, not accuracy.

decisions.decision: Super-resolution is ruled out as a resolution fix.
decisions.reason: No controlled radiograph study shows it restoring task-relevant detail, and the one positive chest report is 400 images with an unclear baseline.

decisions.decision: Proposed label convention: training truth counts from C2 with the 8th segment as T1, the 20th as L1 and the 25th as S1; at inference the morphological 'last mobile' name is reported beside the enumerated one and disagreement is flagged.
decisions.reason: Both conventions appear in the source captions; surgeons act on the morphological name and MRI reports carry the enumerated one, and the choice changes the transitional stratum's accuracy by construction.

decisions.decision: Proposed: the primary endpoint is per-vertebra exact accuracy in the L3-S1 and T10-L2 fields, stratified LSTV versus normal and instrumented versus not, each with a 95% interval; thoracic T2-T9 and cervical are secondary claims; pre-register the convention, strata and sample sizes before the first Tier 0 frame is labelled.
decisions.reason: Every wrong-level event in 34,544 cases occurred at L4/5 or L5/S1; an overall 99% averaged across regions would hide a thoracic figure below 60.

artifacts.title: Spinal Border Variants
artifacts.readme_summary: Spinal border variants (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: No date, stamp or 'as of' line anywhere in the page; the only version marker is the data folder named in the footer, 'Measurements from data/v5_final'.
artifacts.question: Across the 802 densified CTSpinoPelvic1K cases, does a variant at the thoracolumbar border (rib 12, lumbar ribs) predict a variant at the lumbosacral border (LSTV), and which segmentation-derived measures carry that phenotype?
artifacts.summary: A results page over CTSpinoPelvic1K's 802 densified cases that measures the thoracolumbar and lumbosacral borders separately from the segmentation and tests whether a variant at one end predicts one at the other: it does, with an odds ratio of 19.6, 44 cases carrying both where independence predicts 9 (of 796 with complete measurements: 667 typical at both ends, 60 thoracolumbar only, 25 lumbosacral only). Three findings are kept: rib 12 length as a fraction of rib 11 is bimodal (modes near 0.68 and 0.32, 67 cases below 0.30); labelled LSTV cases sit at four (35) or six (26) free lumbar vertebrae instead of the cohort's five (734); and the thoracolumbar measure rib12_len_left_mm separates the lumbosacral LSTV label with d about 0.55. A table of Cohen's d ranks has_l6_label (4.7), n_non_rib_bearing (0.8), rib ratios (0.3 to 0.5), sacral size (-0.3) and Castellvi proxies (under 0.2). Caveats: the sacral foramina counts from the detector are unusable as anatomy (3 left and 7 right on one symmetric sacrum) and were excluded from the co-occurrence test; the Castellvi axes are proxies not grades; the 33 of 802 LSTV labels are an imperfect reference. A rib renumbering done alongside cut ribs on the wrong vertebra from 109 to 19 by giving lumbar ribs their own class (74 and 75), and seven cases are listed as needing a person.

key_claims.claim: A thoracolumbar variant strongly predicts a lumbosacral variant: odds ratio 19.6, 44 cases with both where independence predicts 9.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Cases with a thoracolumbar variant carry a lumbosacral variant 44 times, where independence predicts 9 .

key_claims.claim: This is the 'one population, not two' claim made countable, but it is an association in segmentation-derived measures, not a causal or clinical result.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: This is the “one population, not two” claim, made countable. It is an association in segmentation-derived measures, not a causal or clinical result.

key_claims.claim: Every measure is derived from the segmentation rather than from the vertebra numbering, because counting up from the sacrum begs the question when the sacrum is what changed.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: counting up from the sacrum begs the question when the sacrum is what changed.

key_claims.claim: Rib 12 length as a fraction of rib 11 is bimodal, a main population near 0.68 and a hypoplastic one near 0.32, which is what a discrete developmental variant should look like.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: a main population near 0.68 and a distinct hypoplastic population near 0.32 . 67 cases fall below 0.30 .

key_claims.claim: Labelled LSTV cases avoid five free lumbar vertebrae, sitting at four (35) and six (26) while the cohort piles at five (734); the 13 lumbar-rib cases cluster at four.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The cohort piles at five ( 734 cases). Labelled LSTV cases sit at four ( 35 ) and six ( 26 ) instead

key_claims.claim: A thoracolumbar measure, rib12_len_left_mm, separates the lumbosacral LSTV label with d above 0.5, the co-occurrence showing a second way.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: rib12_len_left_mm clears d = 0.5 — a measurement taken at the other end of the spine from the thing being labelled.

key_claims.claim: The sacral foramina counts from the detector are unusable as anatomy: small canals close in a bone mask and morphological closing invents others.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On one symmetric sacrum it returned 3 left and 7 right. Small canals close in a bone mask and morphological closing invents others.

key_claims.claim: The Castellvi lateral span and gap axes are proxies, not grades, so their flat effect sizes may reflect the proxy rather than the anatomy.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: they are not a graded read, and the flat effect sizes may reflect the proxy rather than the anatomy.

key_claims.claim: The LSTV labels are the reference and are imperfect, so effect sizes inherit their errors; 33 of 802 carry a non-normal label.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 33 of 802 carry a non-normal label. ... Effect sizes are measured against this reference, so they inherit its errors.

key_claims.claim: TotalSegmentator numbered the rib cages from the bottom, so a 13th rib on L1 took the id the T12 rib needed; a lumbar-rib class of its own freed the sequence and cut ribs on the wrong vertebra from 109 to 19.

artifacts.title: FluoroCap Pipeline Map
artifacts.readme_summary: Map of the FluoroCap pipeline (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header chip 'Pipeline map · 2026-09-14' and footer 'Generated with the repository at commit of 2026-09-14 (private)'.
artifacts.question: How do the pieces of FluoroCap fit together across six lanes (sources, ingest, evidence, decision, learning loops, serving), what does each stage wait for, and why is each safe to rerun?
artifacts.summary: A map of the FluoroCap pipeline in six lanes: images come in from every reachable captioned source (PMC, aggregators, OpenAlex PDFs, Commons, YouTube with 905 queries, Reddit, Internet Archive with 799 items, patents, sitemaps and Common Crawl, archives), are made into documented panels with a 110-field manifest and DINOv2 duplicate groups, get independent lines of evidence (a YOLO11 pose corner detector, a four-model level ensemble with BiGRU run labeller and flip TTA, EasyOCR printed labels, OCR-guided recovery with SAM, Qwen2.5-VL-7B blind reads, OWLv2 hardware, anatomical anchors rendered as DRRs from CT, a 4-way orientation net), are decoded by decoder v2 into one contiguous run per panel scored by floored model probability plus caption, OCR, hardware, anchors, VLM and figure/video mates, go to reader pages with two readers and adjudication, and are frozen with SHA256SUMS before any claim. Learning loops are detector self-training (Noisy Student), FluoroGen (SDXL + ControlNet + LoRA restyling DRRs into C-arm frames), anchor detector training on 3,000+ rendered views, level-model arms in Slurm arrays, and nnU-Net v2 CT segmentation folds. Serving is a FastAPI level service in Docker with private weights. A Mermaid diagram and a table give the synchronisation: every stage is a Slurm job or a login-node orchestrator polling for a file or job name, outputs are JSON lines named by run tag, and the filesystem is the contract. An environments table names spineps, spinedet, fluorogen, totalseg, a Singularity image and WSL on the workstation.

artifacts.title: Naming Vertebrae Without CT
artifacts.readme_summary: Naming vertebrae without CT (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Dateline '18 September 2026 · every figure below is measured on spines the system was not trained on'.
artifacts.question: Can a short C-arm sweep plus morphology-based naming identify the vertebral level on a later limited-field spot film without a CT, and how does each of the six steps of that chain perform on held-out spines?
artifacts.summary: A results page for registration-free vertebral level identification from the C-arm: a short sweep of overlapping exposures builds a map of the patient's own spine, later spot films are matched onto it by correlation and named from morphology, never from a count. The headline is that a three-vertebra spot film with no landmark is named correctly 93.9% of the time on the sweep against 85.7% alone (90.4% with the automatic detector rather than human boxes). The page walks the six-step chain (sweep with two bodies of overlap: chain intact 88.3% to 97.5%; a class-agnostic detector finding 97.6% of bodies with the sacrum given its own detector at 98.2% precision / 96.9% recall; box repair from local spacing cutting in-frame duplicates from 3.03% to 0.61%; majority rather than unanimity in frame linking cutting cross-frame duplicates from 21.8% to 3.0% and lifting chain naming from 67.4% to 91.8%; chain naming 100% on real film and 95.0% on CT renders; spot-film placement). It gives per-region two-vertebra figures (cervical and upper thoracic 0% alone to 100% swept), a widened cranial-anchor table (oblique renders fall to about 58%), a re-implemented comparison on 1,653 films and 8,422 vertebrae (counting paradigms abstain on 97-98%, this work 97.0% exact), and a literature comparator table (surgeons unassisted 69.6%, with CT overlay 97.6%). Transitional performance is declared unmeasured (eight held-out spines, one six-lumbar named wrongly), a cross-validation over 376 transitional patients is running, and the reading programme is argued for because only real six-lumbar examples ever moved that class (67.4% to 73.5% after 83 real images). Design decisions, a planned reader study of assisted naming, and plainly stated limits close it; it is marked not for distribution outside the group.

key_claims.claim: A three-vertebra spot film with no landmark is named correctly far more often once matched onto the sweep than on its own pixels.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: named correctly 93.9% of the time once matched onto the sweep, against 85.7% judged on its own pixels. With the automatic vertebra-finder in the loop rather than a human's boxes, 90.4%

key_claims.claim: Two bodies of overlap is the right sweep protocol; more exposures make the chain worse.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: half a body completes the chain on 88.3% of spines, one body 96.7%, two bodies 97.5%, four bodies 82.5% — worse, at more than twice the exposures

key_claims.claim: The general detector's misses concentrate on the sacrum and are not recoverable by lowering the threshold.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the miss rate is 2.42% at confidence 0.25, 0.10 and 0.05 alike, so those bodies are not sitting just below the cut

key_claims.claim: A single-class sacrum detector trained on patient-split data recovers the anchor.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Trained on the 4,526 images that carry a sacrum box, single class, split by patient: precision 98.2%, recall 96.9%

key_claims.claim: Box repair from local spacing, never from a count, removes most duplicate bodies and closes over half the gap to human boxes.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: takes duplicated bodies from 3.03% to 0.61% and naming from 83.0 / 85.6 / 90.2 to 87.2 / 90.4 / 91.4% at two, three and four vertebrae

key_claims.claim: The published lumbar baseline's fixed-cardinality decode fails structurally on six-lumbar and fused spines.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: it decodes exactly five boxes because 'the human spine typically consists of five lumbar vertebrae', and its own authors report the consequence — on a six-lumbar spine it drops a vertebra

key_claims.claim: Requiring a majority rather than unanimity when linking frames removed the project's largest error.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Requiring a majority rather than unanimity took duplication from 21.8% to 3.0% and chain naming from 67.4% to 91.8%

key_claims.claim: Once the chain is right, every vertebra in it is named correctly on held-out real film.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On held-out real film every vertebra in the chain is named correctly on 100% of films; on CT renders, 95.0%.

key_claims.claim: The further a frame sits from a landmark, the more the sweep is worth.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: In the cervical and upper thoracic spine a two-vertebra frame is named correctly essentially never on its own ... and essentially always once placed on the map

key_claims.claim: Transitional-spine performance is unmeasured, not poor.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: eight spines with transitional anatomy remain, and exactly one with six lumbar vertebrae — which the system named wrongly. Eight spines cannot distinguish 60% from 95%

key_claims.claim: Oblique projections are markedly harder, which matters because a C-arm is rarely square to the patient.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the chain completes on 74% of them and naming falls to about 58%

key_claims.claim: Counting paradigms score near zero on tight fields because they abstain, which is the clinical problem this work removes.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: with no landmark in a tight field there is nothing to count from, so they abstain on 97–98% of frames

key_claims.claim: The clinical comparator is an assisted surgeon, and nothing on the page answers whether this system brings a surgeon to CT-overlay accuracy without a CT.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: does a surgeon assisted by this system reach the accuracy of a surgeon assisted by CT registration, in cases that have no CT? ... nothing here answers it yet

key_claims.claim: Only real six-lumbar examples ever moved the six-lumbar number; every algorithmic fix moved nothing.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Then 83 real clinical images of six-lumbar spines entered training and accuracy at that vertebra went from 67.4% to 73.5% on held-out patients.

key_claims.claim: Pseudolabels agree with human readers on ordinary spines but cost anomalous accuracy, so the deployed configuration excludes them.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: training on them cost twenty points of anomalous accuracy, which is why the deployed configuration excludes them

key_claims.claim: An earlier version of this work reported figures that included spines the model was trained on; an audit found it.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: An earlier version of this work reported figures that did not have that property; the audit that found it is recorded in the repository.

key_claims.claim: No partially lumbarised S1 label exists anywhere in the corpus.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: 5,110 images carry a sacrum box and zero carry an S1 box — so no model can currently be asked to place one

key_claims.claim: Surgeons unaided on difficult C-arm films name the level correctly about seven times in ten; with a CT-registration overlay nearly always.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A surgeon working unaided on difficult C-arm films names the level correctly 69.6% of the time. The same surgeon with a CT-registration overlay reaches 97.6%

artifacts.question: Which credentials and access routes should the owner obtain, in what order, and where should they be stored so the FluoroCap harvesters can fetch larger figure renditions and social-media sources without any secret being printed or committed?
artifacts.summary: A ranked setup page for the FluoroCap figure-harvesting corpus. It opens with the free fix already running: publishers' own sites hold larger renditions than PMC, their figure URLs are deterministic from the DOI for five publishers, and the measured gains on real corpus figures run from 4x (Springer, BMC, Nature) to 16x (Cureus); 18 of 21 test figures were replaced, the 3 failures being on SAGE. It then lays out the hand-over mechanism (a mode-600 file ~/.fluorocap/credentials.env filled in an editor, cookie jars, an Instagram session; tools/fluorocap_creds.py init and check report names and pass/fail only), the free API keys worth about five minutes each (NCBI, YouTube, Springer, Elsevier, Flickr, Reddit, Google CSE, PatentsView), Wayne State institutional access (campus IP first, proxy cookie second, with cautions about the 30 June 2026 library note and publisher licences), Instagram on a dedicated account at 8 to 20 seconds per post, Facebook as unreliable, and X/Twitter and TikTok as not worth buying. It ends with the order to do things in and the repository files that hold the same content.

artifacts.title: Lift Before Label?
artifacts.readme_summary: Whether to lift before labelling (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header 'FluoroCap · prior art · 15 September 2026' and the method note 'returned 173 sourced findings on 15 September 2026'.
artifacts.question: Should the FluoroCap identifier reconstruct a frame in 3-D before naming the vertebral level, can CT-to-fluoroscopy registration supply labelled training frames, and would paired synthetic CT editing widen the data?
artifacts.summary: A prior-art synthesis from four literature sweeps (173 sourced findings) answering three questions for the FluoroCap level identifier. On lifting to 3-D before classification the answer is no: no paper reconstructs a radiograph to 3-D then classifies with a gain over the 2-D classifier, single-view lifting is a prior-driven completion that erases exactly the transitional features the label depends on, and what helps instead is 3-D knowledge inside the 2-D model (two-view fusion, physics and randomisation in the renderer, correspondence pretraining). On registration as a data source the answer is yes: registering the patient's CT to the frame labels the real frame, which beats its DRR twin as training data, and the page budgets hundreds to low thousands of registered frames from at least 10 to 20 patients. On paired synthetic editing the answer is partly: hardware insertion is mature, lesion synthesis is proven only for 3-D segmentation, and transitional-variant or corpectomy editing has never been published and is worth a week. It closes with an ordered plan, open questions, and a caveat that the adversarial verification pass did not run.

key_claims.claim: No published work reconstructs a radiograph or C-arm frame to 3-D and then classifies with a gain over a 2-D classifier; a reconstruction stage should not be built.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: No paper anywhere reconstructs a radiograph or C-arm frame to 3-D and then classifies, and reports a gain over the 2-D classifier

key_claims.claim: The only lift-then-decide gain in X-ray-to-CT is chest X-ray to CTPA for pulmonary embolism, and its mechanism does not transfer here.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: AUC 0.691→0.803 with 898 real paired patients and a generator trained on >7,000 disease-bearing CTPAs; X-ray2CTPA, npj Digit Med 2025

decisions.decision: Do not build a reconstruction stage; keep the direct 2-D identifier and use both views when the C-arm gives both.
decisions.reason: No published lift-then-classify gain exists, and single-view lifting completes transitional anatomy toward the typical spine.

decisions.decision: Build the registration route, label every real frame that registers, keep the DRR twin only as augmentation, and fine-tune the identifier on real frames.
decisions.reason: Registration labels real frames, and real frames beat their DRR twins as training data (4.89 vs 7.83 mm).

decisions.decision: Hardware editing stays; transitional and corpectomy CT editing is worth a week; do not generate whole CTs.
decisions.reason: Hardware insertion is validated on real frames, transitional editing is unpublished but cheap with existing label maps, and 3-D generation rendered to DRRs underperforms.

decisions.decision: Do not build a single-view reconstruction stage, a 3-D CT generator, or an img2img translator.
decisions.reason: The evidence says each costs more than it returns.

artifacts.title: Overnight: The Honest 99%
artifacts.readme_summary: Overnight run and its honest accuracy (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header 'FluoroCap · overnight, 15–16 September 2026'; the page reports an overnight run of 15 to 16 September.
artifacts.question: What accuracy can the FluoroCap vertebral-level model honestly promise, at what coverage, and what does the night's work say to do next?
artifacts.summary: An overnight report from nine agents on the FluoroCap level-naming model. It reports accuracy as a pair, accuracy among answered and coverage: 99% right on the 35.7% of vertebrae it names exactly, 99% at 55.7% coverage for a region, and conformal prediction at a 1% error rate giving one region on 70.3% of vertebrae at 99.7%, all on held-out renders. The transitional flag does not improve with more positives (0.652 at ten, 0.713 at 120), and on 3,600 real radiographs it reads age and exposure, not anatomy, while a sex control transfers. Two defects were found: an abstention rule that abstained on the Castellvi IIIb positives it should protect, and label-map errors in VerSeFusion and record 1043. Two benches await the owner (179 panels of 865 vertebrae; 585 transitional figures), the corpus is tabled (20,700 panels, 12,106 figures), a PRISMA-ScR scoping review lost its hypothesis and found that level-determination countermeasures are never evaluated against an outcome, and the next steps are the verification bench, an ordinal loss, real-film calibration, a Castellvi I abstain class and a selective-prediction paper.

artifacts.question: What goes into each page of the WSU eProtocol IRB form for Protocol 1, a retrospective DMC imaging and records study that validates vertebral level naming (CT, registration-labelled intraoperative fluoroscopy, radiographs) and fracture detection, and which items the PI still has to decide?
artifacts.summary: A draft of the first of two WSU IRB eProtocols, laid out in the order of the eProtocol form so each block pastes into its page: an Exempt Category 4 retrospective study at the Detroit Medical Center with a waiver of consent (45 CFR 46.116(f)) and of HIPAA authorization, requesting about 40,000 imaging studies from roughly 25,000 adults from 1 January 2006 to the approval date. Aim 2 is rewritten so that intraoperative fluoroscopy-CT pairs are a named data source and 3-D to 2-D registration of each intraoperative image to the same patient's CT supplies the reference level labels; five hypotheses (H1 to H5) cover CT level naming, registration labels, a registration-free model, fracture detection and registry outcomes. It gives the background figures (wrong-level surgery 0.12% of 34,544 cases, LSTV prevalence 15.3%, LevelCheck 398 of 398), the statistical methods (Wilson intervals, strata by anatomy, region and instrumentation), a sample-size argument (about 1,500 verified vertebrae per stratum, 6,000 in all, 400 fractured studies), the de-identification procedure (DICOM PS3.15 profile, OCR screening and 100% visual inspection of frames, 10% audit of text) and the confidentiality, consent and HIPAA waiver pages. A list of open items (faculty sponsor, radiology co-investigator, the records count, retention wording) and notes to the PI follow, including a commercialisation disclosure that belongs in the eProtocol and nowhere public, and what to cut (Aim 4) if the IRB pushes back.

artifacts.question: What was decided this session for the spine program's paper, network architecture, data and governance, and what can be built on the radiograph corpus as it now stands?
artifacts.summary: The page lists the session's decisions with status: one network with four heads and per-head loss masking rather than one flat class list (locked); level identity on a head reading pooled box features, never on the detector, since C3 appears only in CSXA and T7 only in AASCE (locked); adding CSXA so cervical levels are covered by two independent sources and a train-here/test-there experiment can run (locked); one training fold while debugging after five folds slowed each other and fold 2 died on a 16 GB V100 (in effect); gating figure records on plate orientation rather than on the pelvic-tilt value (locked); withholding L5 from the end-plate and pedicle-width panels (locked); licensing enforced in src/licensing.py (in effect); Spinal-AI2024 pulled for having no licence file (revisit); IRB correspondence purged from public history with git-filter-repo (done). A corpus table totals 50,887 annotated images against 4,327 in the current training set, which scores mAP50 0.991 and PCK@0.1 0.812. A ladder of what can be built follows (level head, LSTV flag, slip grade, Cobb angle, pathology on research track, the DRR transfer experiment). The one open question is L6 scoring Dice 0.00 in every run, with about 22 of 802 cases carrying an L6.

artifacts.title: Counting Against Two Anchors
artifacts.readme_summary: Counting levels against two anchors (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: No date, 'as of', chip or run stamp appears in the text; the only provenance line is 'Full derivation in docs/ANCHOR_ORDINAL_DESIGN.md'.
artifacts.question: How can a segmentation network enumerate vertebrae correctly in transitional anatomy when it is trained almost entirely on normal anatomy?
artifacts.summary: A training-design page for single-pass LSTV and TLTV labelling on CTSpinoPelvic1K (802 CT records with spine, pelvis, per-level ribs and femurs in one frame). It argues that predicting a level name is the wrong target, since a sixth lumbar vertebra occurs in roughly 2% of people and a model learns to call every lowest lumbar vertebra L5; instead two dense ordinal heads predict n_up (vertebrae above the sacrum) and n_down (below the lowest rib-bearing vertebra), the name is derived, and an anomaly is detected as disagreement |n_up + n_down - K|, a self-supervised constraint that holds on every normal case. Because a lumbar rib and a sacralisation shift that sum identically, it proposes four morphological anchors (costal facets, rib articulation, SI articulation, promontory) whose pattern of disagreement is a signature naming the variant, plus a thoracic-versus-lumbar morphology head that repairs the rib anchor when the twelfth rib is aplastic (T12 separates from L1 at AUC 0.990, 97.3% over 1485 vertebrae). It names the patch tension (a 112 x 112 x 320 column-spanning patch at 4.01 Mvox cannot span the 309 mm pelvis, and anisotropy blurs the 2-4 mm costotransverse joint), resolves it with a cascade, lists five experimental arms with arms 1 and 2 as the matched pair the argument turns on, and lists the metrics to report instead of Dice. It closes by recording that sacral foramina failed as an anchor because their count in normal-labelled cases (mode 3, not 4) overlaps the variants, dominated by field of view.

key_claims.claim: Predicting a level name directly is the wrong target: the model is rewarded for never predicting L6, a property of the target and not the backbone.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: This is the documented failure mode, and it is a property of the target , not the backbone. Oversampling fights the symptom. The target has to change.

key_claims.claim: Two ordinal counts from opposite anchors (sacrum and lowest rib-bearing vertebra) let the name be derived and the anomaly be detected as disagreement, learned from the normal cases.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Both counting functions are learned from the 97% of cases that are normal.

key_claims.claim: The sum n_up + n_down cannot distinguish a lumbar rib from a sacralisation, since both reduce it by one.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A lumbar rib and a sacralisation both reduce n_up + n_down by one. The sum cannot tell them apart.

key_claims.claim: Four morphological anchors are perturbed by different variant families, so the pattern of disagreement is a signature that names the variant and decomposes a case with both a lumbar rib and a sacralisation.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: rib variants perturb {A, B} and leave {C, D}; sacral variants perturb {C, D} and leave {A, B}.

key_claims.claim: Thoracic and lumbar vertebrae separate by shape alone on this corpus at AUC 0.990 and 97.3% accuracy over 1485 vertebrae.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: T12 separates from L1 at AUC 0.990 and 97.3% accuracy over 1485 vertebrae, using shape alone with each patient's own size divided out.

key_claims.claim: A tall narrow 112 x 112 x 320 patch at 1 mm spans the column in 4.01 Mvox, cheaper than nnU-Net's default 192 cubed at 7.08, but cannot span the pelvis's 309 mm p95 width.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A tall narrow patch, 112 × 112 × 320 at 1 mm, spans the column in 4.01 Mvox — cheaper than nnU-Net's default 192³ at 7.08. The pelvis needs 309 mm of width at p95

key_claims.claim: The consistency penalty |n_up + n_down - K| is a self-supervised constraint that applies to every case, including those with no transitional label.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: In normal anatomy this is a self-supervised constraint that holds on every case — so it applies to all the data, including the cases carrying no transitional label at all.

key_claims.claim: Sacral foramina are not a usable anchor on this corpus: the count in normal-labelled cases has mode three and overlaps the labelled variants, dominated by field of view.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The mode is three, not four , and the distribution overlaps the labelled sacralisations and lumbarisations completely. The measurement is dominated by field of view

key_claims.claim: The delta between arm 1 (semantic heads only) and arm 2 (plus ordinal heads and consistency loss) on the same folds is the result the design turns on.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Run arms 1 and 2 as a matched pair on the same folds. The delta between them is the result.

key_claims.claim: Count accuracy must be split by typical and transitional anatomy, since an overall figure hides a null result on the transitional cases.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A model 97% accurate overall and 0% on transitional cases is the null result in costume, and only the split reveals it.

decisions.decision: The target changes from a level name to two ordinal counts (n_up from the sacrum, n_down from the lowest rib-bearing vertebra) with the name derived.
decisions.reason: A name-predicting model is rewarded for never predicting L6 (about 2% prevalence) and calls every lowest lumbar vertebra L5; the defect is in the target, not the backbone, and oversampling only fights the symptom.

decisions.decision: Anchors are chosen by morphology (costal facets, rib articulation, SI articulation, promontory) so that each variant family perturbs a different subset.
decisions.reason: Every count anchor is perturbed by the variants it should detect, and a lumbar rib and a sacralisation shift n_up + n_down identically.

decisions.decision: A third per-voxel head predicts thoracic versus lumbar type from morphology, repairing the rib anchor when the twelfth rib is aplastic; the vertebra names the rib.
decisions.reason: With an aplastic twelfth rib n_down has no origin, and the costal facet is present in hundreds of training thoracic vertebrae (T12 vs L1 at AUC 0.990).

decisions.decision: Ordinal regression is used rather than plain regression for the count heads.
decisions.reason: The targets are small ordered integers; rank-consistent formulations respect that where an L2 loss does not.

decisions.decision: The cascade (3d_cascade_fullres) is the principled resolution of the patch tension: a low-resolution stage locates sacral anchors against the whole pelvis and a full-resolution stage resolves the costal facet.
decisions.reason: The ordinal heads need a column-spanning receptive field (265 mm) and the morphology classes need native detail (2-4 mm joint); no single patch serves both.

decisions.decision: Arms 1 and 2 are run as a matched pair on the same folds; their delta is the result.
decisions.reason: It isolates the contribution of the ordinal formulation from that of the architecture, the comparison the whole argument turns on.

decisions.decision: Sacral foramina are ruled out as anchor C.
decisions.reason: Across 802 records the foramina count in normal-labelled cases has mode three and overlaps the labelled sacralisations and lumbarisations completely, dominated by field of view.

decisions.decision: Rib-free count accuracy is reported split by typical and transitional anatomy, with anchor-agreement calibration (an ROC on the scalar), stump-rib recall and the failure mode, rather than Dice.
decisions.reason: Dice would hide a model 97% accurate overall and 0% on transitional cases.

open_questions: Whether the ordinal heads plus consistency loss (arm 2) beat the semantic-only baseline (arm 1) on the same folds; the arms are listed, not run.
Whether the cascade in fact serves both the counting heads and the morphology classes, given that they want different patches.
Whether PrimusV2's positional embeddings help where long-range ordering is the entire task.
Stump-rib recall, the case where the rib anchor fails and morphology carries it alone.
Whether |n_up + n_down - K| separates transitional from typical anatomy on this corpus (the ROC is proposed, not reported).
Whether the SI-articulation anchor moves under Castellvi III-IV and lumbarisation ('may move').

Four pairs of sacral foramina is normal and five means an absorbed lumbar segment is called the textbook anchor without a citation.

artifacts.question: Are the vertebral levels the FluoroCap decode pipeline assigned to 120 stratified panels correct, as judged by a human reader who reads the film before seeing the caption?
artifacts.summary: The page is a single-reader adjudication bench over 120 FluoroCap panels drawn stratified across the pipeline's deciding evidence (caption, model, mate, ocr, vlm, hardware, none, anchor) and spinal region (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral), with or without a caption. For each panel it shows the image with invert, boost and zoom controls, what the pipeline decided (the decoded levels with per-level confidences, the decider, the box count, whether the order was reversed, whether the caption was forced, the region drawn and the id), and a caption the reader may reveal, recording whether it was revealed. The reader picks one of five verdicts (levels correct, off by one level, wrong by more than one, cannot tell, not a spine radiograph), may type the correct levels and a note, and the reads are saved to the artifact's shared record through the db capability when it connects, else to the browser's localStorage. The item data comes from decode_v2_v2.jsonl under the batch tag b1; 93 panels come from PMC figure panels (with captions) and 27 from video panels (without). No verdicts or results are present in the page.

The extracted text cut the page's script data mid-JSON (after "none|lumbar|no"), so the full strata_counts and the 120-item array were read from the artifact's own index.html, a text file (66,333 bytes); the per-item decoded levels and confidences were tallied, not transcribed. artifacts.question: What moved in the spine program (dataset paper, CT fold training, radiograph corpus, architecture and licensing) as of 11 September 2026, and what waits on the owner?
artifacts.summary: A status board as of 11 Sep 2026 09:05 EDT: on the grid, spine_train fold 4 resumed at epoch 50 on an H200 at about 910 s per epoch, xr_build is normalising about 22,000 radiographs into one manifest, the dl_nhanes chain was cancelled with 17,073 of 17,075 files down, and folds 0 to 3 were stopped deliberately (fold 2 had been handed a 16 GB V100 against a 100 GB plan). The dataset paper (10 pages, pushed to both remotes) got five fixes: canal depth was measuring the wrong chord on the wrong slice (473 to 12 records below 11 mm), 128 low pelvic incidences were a plate leaning backwards (39/39 vs 0/39, 140 plates rejected on geometry, table II n 563 with PI 52.7 SS 33.2 PT 19.7), L5 withheld for end-plate and pedicle width, recumbency's effect on sacral slope corrected against Hasegawa, Figure 5 reverted to one CT line, and a hardcoded rib base fixed (237 of 802 records moved). The radiograph corpus grows from 4,327 toward about 13,500: the CSXA converter yields 24,815 named cervical vertebrae on 4,963 films, and BUU ships unused LSTV truth (3,461 / 15 / 130, 4.0%) and slip grades (465 grade-3, 194 grade-4). Architecture: one backbone, four heads, level identity on a head; a licensing table checked against primary sources is enforced in src/licensing.py. Waiting on the owner: purging public IRB files, BUU commercial permission, and a competing group (Barr et al.) already on CSXA.

decisions.decision: Level identity goes on a head, never on the detector; one backbone, four heads, not one flat class list (decided).
decisions.reason: A flat class list teaches false negatives and a detector with level classes learns dataset signature; a head on pooled per-instance features sees only the vertebra.

decisions.decision: Folds 0 to 3 stopped deliberately; fold 4 runs alone on an H200.
decisions.reason: Five folds in parallel made each other slow: the first stages to NVMe, the rest fall back to NFS.

decisions.decision: The dl_nhanes chain was cancelled.
decisions.reason: It was resubmitting itself every 5 minutes forever with 17,073 of 17,075 files already down and two permanently dead.

decisions.decision: Canal depth fixed to a midsagittal chord at the pedicle plane.
decisions.reason: The old measure took the widest chord of the first closed ring, which on a trefoil L4/L5 canal ran through a lateral recess.

decisions.decision: Plates are rejected on geometry (orientation of the normal), not on the pelvic-incidence value; 140 rejected.
decisions.reason: The tilt gate is blind to the direction of tilt; where the S1 carve fails the plane fits the ventral sacrum with a posteriorly leaning normal.

decisions.decision: L5 withheld for end-plate and pedicle width; the row is dropped and the text says why.
decisions.reason: Contamination from cutting at the canal wall is confined to L5 and large there; three replacement rules did not beat the shipping one.

decisions.decision: The manuscript's statement that recumbency lowers sacral slope was corrected to raises.
decisions.reason: Hasegawa's table gives supine 34.1 degrees against standing 27.0.

decisions.decision: Figure 5 reverted to one published CT line; Table II carries both series.
decisions.reason: Drawing Hasegawa beside Veilleux gave 24 deformity patients the same visual weight as 200 asymptomatic subjects with no n on the figure.

decisions.decision: Rib bases are read from the scheme shipped beside the labels instead of a hardcoded constant.
decisions.reason: Two label directories have rib blocks that differ by one; the constant moved rib12_to_crest_mm in 237 of 802 records.

artifacts.title: Rib Anchor Audit
artifacts.readme_summary: Audit of rib anchors (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: No date line, chip or stamp in the text; the only version marker is 'CTSpinoPelvic1K · v4 → v5'.
artifacts.question: Did merging the reviewed ribs and thoracic spine into CTSpinoPelvic1K v5 fix the rib numbering errors, and can grouping vertebrae by rib-bearing retire the naming argument and agree with a radiologist?
artifacts.summary: On 802 cases and 11,579 ribs, v5 = v4 plus 169 rib and 107 thoracic spine reviews, merged anatomy-pure by id range. Scoring each rib against the vertebra its number claims (within 10 mm), numbering errors fell 170 to 109 (down 36%) and the targeted -1 shift 129 to 71, while the +1 arm barely moved, the signature of a real correction; lumbar ribs rose 21 to 25, so anomalies were preserved. Two QC bugs of the author's own inflated rib-count asymmetry: 230 of 801 cases was field-of-view truncation (228 of 236 unmatched ribs touch the top slice), and excluding truncated ribs singly still gave 112; excluding by rib number on both sides gives 15 (1.9%), and 57% of ribs are clipped. Counting non-rib-bearing vertebrae between the last rib and the sacrum returns 5 in 93.3% of cases but agrees with the radiologist on only 2 of 22, because the labels assign L1 to L5 plus a sacrum by convention, so the count recovers the convention, not the patient. Two mask-based sacral tests (ilium contact with L5, sacroiliac height against the S1 endplate) are proposed as a second anchor; v5 is a local tree on the grid and nothing is pushed to HuggingFace.

decisions.decision: Truncated ribs are excluded from counts by rib number on both sides, never individually.
decisions.reason: Excluding truncated ribs one at a time manufactures the asymmetry it is meant to remove (112 asymmetric cases remained).

decisions.decision: A vertebra is rib-bearing only when it is that rib's single nearest vertebra, not merely within 10 mm.
decisions.reason: Proximity is not articulation: a 12th rib head is within 10 mm of both T12 and L1, marking L1 rib-bearing in 61 cases against 14 lumbar ribs found by strict incidence.

decisions.decision: Indeterminate cases (20) are excluded rather than undercounted.
decisions.reason: A missing level would fabricate a sacralization.

decisions.decision: The 93.3 / 3.3 / 3.3 count distribution is not to be quoted as a phenotype prevalence.
decisions.reason: It is largely the label convention: labels assign L1 to L5 plus a sacrum regardless of true anatomy.

decisions.decision: A vertebra anchors a rib only at 6,000 voxels or more; rib incidence is within 10 mm; a misnumbered case is 3 or more ribs at one consistent delta.
decisions.reason: An FOV-edge sliver cannot claim a rib whose true vertebra is out of view; 10 mm separates the right vertebra from an off-by-one neighbour; one stray offset is a segmentation artefact.

decisions.decision: The paper's framing: record evidence and disagreement rather than a name, since a lumbosacral field of view cannot resolve vertebral identity in principle.
decisions.reason: There is no imaging gold standard for vertebral identity on a lumbosacral field; counting from C2 on whole-spine imaging is the only definitive method.

decisions.decision: Next: two mask-based sacral tests (ilium contact with the L5 transverse process; sacroiliac articulation height against the labelled S1 endplate), calibrated where rib and sacral anchors agree.
decisions.reason: Both fail for different reasons than rib counting, so where they agree numbering is settled and where they disagree the transitional cohort triages itself.

artifacts.title: Registration-Free Level ID Feasibility
artifacts.readme_summary: Feasibility of registration-free level identification (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Subtitle line 'Deep research · 102 agents · adversarially verified · 15 September 2026'.
artifacts.question: Is a registration-free single-frame vertebral level classifier feasible on real radiographs or fluoroscopy, given the published evidence?
artifacts.summary: A deep-research page (102 agents, each claim voted on by three verifiers, two refutations killing a claim) that answers whether a registration-free vertebral level classifier is feasible. Its verdict is narrow: no surviving claim gives a per-level identification accuracy for a registration-free single-frame system on real radiographs or fluoroscopy; the only registration-free labeller in scope (Huang et al. 2022, trained on images synthesised from 297 CTs and tested on 50 AP + 50 lateral cadaveric Long-Film images from 13 specimens) survived only as a protocol description, its 88.3% and 3.3 mm figures refuted. What is established is a ceiling on the harder sub-task: a single lateral lumbar film can flag LSTV presence (ResNet-50 on 3,116 films: accuracy 76.4%, sensitivity 85.1%, specificity 61.9%, AUC 0.84, below a specialist at 83.9%) but cannot assign a Castellvi type (radiograph readers 32% sensitivity, 42% accuracy; 35.2% of AP subtypes disagree with CT), and clinicians miscount levels in 54% (38/71) of LSTV patients on limited-field imaging. The comparator LevelCheck needs a preoperative CT and 3D-2D registration, placed labels within the correct level on all 398 radiographs after excluding 21, was judged helpful in 42.2% of cases (thoracic 77.7%, lumbar 33.5%) and has never shown a reduction in wrong-level error. Eight findings survived; the realistic promise is a binary LSTV/TLTV/atypical-count flag with abstention when the sacrum, odontoid or twelfth rib is out of field. Four open questions and a caveats paragraph on coverage gaps close the page.

open_questions: What per-level accuracy does a registration-free CNN reach on real (not cadaveric, not Long-Film) C-arm fluoroscopy and plain films, by region, and how much of the gap is sim-to-real versus intrinsic ambiguity of mid-thoracic and lumbosacral levels?

Can local morphology on a single AP or lateral frame distinguish L6 from L5, T13 from L1, or a lumbarised S1 from L5 when the sacrum or twelfth rib is in the field; is the abstention set defined by field of view alone or also by numerical variants?

Which public or licensable datasets contain real intraoperative spine fluoroscopy or radiographs with whole-spine-verified level labels and transitional-anatomy annotations, under what licences and sizes, and does any include Castellvi-typed LSTV with CT reference?
Does a level-confirmation alert change surgeon behaviour or wrong-level rates in a prospective trial? None has been reported.
The sim-to-real gap for real C-arm frames from DRR training remains unquantified in this evidence set.
unsourced_assertions: 'entirely' simulated and 'no clinical images' for Huang 2022 are the page's own inferences from abstract silence (full text paywalled).

The inference that landmark-confounder cases are exactly those a morphology-based single-frame classifier cannot resolve is the synthesis's own; De Silva et al. say nothing about registration-free classifiers.
The fluoroscopy wording of finding 01 rests on the review's other references, not on Nakagawa's data, which were outpatient radiograph/MRI.
Whether transitional vertebrae were present in Huang's 13 cadavers is not stated.

artifacts.title: FluoroCap Overnight Report
artifacts.readme_summary: FluoroCap overnight report (page)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line: "Overnight report · read at 06:25, updated 08:30 on 15 September 2026, grid time"; the before row of the panel table is dated "14 Sep audit" and the films-only model was "deployed on 14 September".
artifacts.question: What did the FluoroCap pipeline finish, lose, fix and leave running overnight into 15 September 2026, and which corpus and level-model numbers changed?
artifacts.summary: An overnight status page for the FluoroCap pipeline, read at 06:25 and updated 08:30 grid time on 15 September 2026, reporting what finished, what still runs, what broke and the numbers that changed, all read off result files. Round one of the publisher refetch replaced 1,489 of 2,901 figures with larger copies (median 6.3x the pixels), raising the median panel short side from 231 to 320 px and the share at or above 512 px from 7.9% to 23.4%; round two was still running after a WSL disk outage, and Wolters Kluwer, Ovid and Thieme remained blocked pending proxy sessions. The all-spine v1 level model learned the thoracic levels the 14 Sep audit found missing (T10 from 0.0% to 95.8% on CT renders), but its 92.7% all-level render score is called a training-set score; the v2 model, retrained after a link step destroyed its first weights, scores 64.2% on held-out renders, and on six-lumbar spines the models still shift every lumbar name down by one, which the v2 bank's rare-anatomy oversampling and a decoder that inserts T13 or L6 are built to fix. Synthetic frame generation by SDXL img2img was dropped after it erased the vertebrae, the CUT translator's first run was declared invalid for training toward contaminated panels, and a content-addressed model registry replaced ln -sf linking. The page ends with two requests to the owner about proxy cookie exports.

artifacts.question: What is the FluoroCap collection of published intra-operative spine fluoroscopy and radiograph panels with level-naming captions, how was it assembled and licensed, and where does its reference standard stand?
artifacts.summary: FluoroCap is a prospectively defined, reproducible collection of published intra-operative spine fluoroscopy and radiograph figure panels whose captions name the vertebral level, built under a written search-and-inclusion protocol (query strings in eleven languages) for validating vertebral-level identification; one manifest (10,281 rows, manifest version 1.1, dataset version 0.2) yields Dataset A (all open-access tiers, research use) and Dataset B (CC BY, CC0 and public domain only). Each source figure is fetched, hashed, split into panels at the gutters, re-encoded from pixel data with no EXIF or DICOM metadata, hashed again and written as one manifest row carrying source, licence tier, fetch record, modality, levels, devices, population sentences, geometry, inclusion or exclusion reason and subgroup flags; four inclusion criteria (I1 to I4) hold, E1 (no level named) and E5 (classifier below 0.3) exclude, and cadaver/phantom (E4) and licence (E8) are flags only at this version. The reference standard is pending: the level attached to each panel is the author's caption plus a constraint decoder combining caption, named hardware and contiguity with the model's proposal, a proposal for the readers, not ground truth; the protocol calls for two blind readers, third-reader adjudication and locking before any performance claim. Figure mates agree on region 88% of the time with the decoder against 52% for the model alone. v0.1 was frozen; the working manifest will be frozen as v1 with reader labels; version 0.3 (video frames, archive scans, teaching-case sites) is in progress.

artifacts.question: How much of the spine does a model need to see to name a vertebra's exact level, on held-out patients, on real lateral films and on CT projections?
artifacts.summary: A run report on classifiers over 27 levels (C1–L6, T13, sacrum) that scale the target vertebra to a fixed pixel height and shrink the visible context one rung at a time down to a single vertebra, with 30% of patients from every annotated source held out. On real films one vertebra gives 96.7% exact and 99.7% within one level over 8,422 crops; cervical reaches 97.7% (7,900 crops) and lumbar 80.7 to 85.4% (410 crops), rising to 91.9% at three vertebrae. The jump from 84% to 97% came entirely from adding CSXA's 4,963 cervical patients and BUU's 7,200 lumbar films; architecture, absolute size in millimetres, learning rate, epochs and masking moved nothing by more than a few points, and CT-only models transfer 7% to real film. On CT projections the ladder runs from 63.5% at one vertebra to 91.8% with the whole scan, where 80% of the remaining errors are whole-case shifts, so within-one-level is the honest primary metric. An outline of 128 silhouette points matches the image arm on synthetic data. The page says none of this is clinical validation and lists what runs next: the +BUU rungs, VinDr pseudo-labelling as a train-only lumbar source, dual-view fusion and contrastive pretraining.

artifacts.question: Which of the 32 REFORMS reporting items can be enforced as an automated gate in the hpcworker and Beethoven pipeline, where each gate fires, and which repository owns it?
artifacts.summary: The checklist maps all 32 REFORMS items (Kapoor et al.) to a gate, finding 20 verifiable by code and 12 only enforceable as a declared non-empty field in study.yaml. Each gate fires before dispatch, after the run, before publish, or as a declared field, and none exists yet: both repositories are the Remote Control launcher (hpcworker framework 11, extension 12.0.0). Ownership splits three ways because the framework is held to bash 4.2 and Python 3.6 stdlib on the CentOS 7 login node while Hydra, MONAI, W&B and CodeCarbon can only live in the container image: hpcworker takes the run manifest, Run ID, clean-tree refusal and publish lock; a proposed beethoven-research repository takes the schema, splitter, leakage checks, bootstrap CIs and card builders; the extension takes a read-only checklist view and the human Publish approval, through a per-run contract file reforms.json. Four conflicts with CLAUDE.md are listed with fixes (Run ID must not hash Slurm variables, publishing waits for a human click, tokens in a mode-0600 file, LiteLLM key rotation is out), three questions are left for the owner, and a seven-step build order starts with the two gates that need no ML libraries.

artifacts.question: Where can a currently enrolled medical student, with the resident as mentor, ask for money to run OpenSpineConsortium outreach, ordered by how fast it can arrive, and what will each source pay for?
artifacts.summary: A briefing for a medical student in the OSC research year listing twelve funding sources ordered by speed of arrival: local small awards (WSUSOM Student Senate $250 to $400 with a $450 ceiling and no committee cycle; the Student Activities Funding Board for on-campus free public events; the Office of Medical Student Research Scholarly Activity Award up to $500 with a 3-day post-acceptance fast path; SOM Alumni Association funds via Student Affairs), months-long applications (WSU GME Seed Grant up to $2,500, which the resident must apply for and which alone covers materials; the AΩA Service Leadership grant $9,000 over two years, deadline 16 Feb 2027; the Community Foundation for Southeast Michigan, with a $70,000 precedent to a WSU student group), and the radiology societies whose cycles open in October 2026 with deadlines around 1 February (RSNA Research Medical Student Grant $3,000 plus a $3,000 departmental match; RSNA Education Project Award $10,000 to $20,000; the Radiology Education Research Development Grant up to $10,000; SIR student awards; the RSNA Education Scholar Grant up to $75,000 as a later destination). Two structural facts shape it: the resident cannot be the applicant on student awards, and OSC is not a Registered Student Organization, so an existing registered organization should host events with OSC as the program. Every application should cite OSC's record: 802 CT records annotated and openly released, 13 medical students trained as annotators, a peer-reviewed Cureus paper on the education model and two permanent archives. The immediate steps are to confirm enrolment, ask Student Affairs about alumni funds (which makes the Senate request admissible), and settle RSNA membership and the departmental match before October.

key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: ordered by how fast it can actually arrive — not by how much it is. The first seven are local and small; the radiology societies at the end are the opposite, and their window opens next month.

key_claims.claim: The Scholarly Activity Award (up to $500) has a 60-day lead time and a fast path of three days after an abstract acceptance; it funds travel to present, continental US and Canada only.

key_claims.claim: The WSU GME Seed Grant (up to $2,500) is the one source that pays for materials, software and printing; it prohibits travel, registration and publication fees and requires IRB documentation, a faculty mentor's approval and a mentoring plan.

artifacts.question: What is the Celebrate Life soccer night for kids with scoliosis, and when, where, for whom and how do families sign up?
artifacts.summary: A one-page flyer for Celebrate Life, a soccer night for kids with scoliosis at the Detroit City Fieldhouse on Saturday, October 24 from 5:00 to 7:00 PM, held at the same time as the Fieldhouse's Turf or Treat event, with two indoor fields side by side, one given over to trick-or-treating and one to soccer coached by professional players from Southeast Michigan. Every kid under 18 living with scoliosis or a spine condition may play, whether bracing, being watched and waited on, or after surgery with their surgeon's OK; families are welcome on the sideline, costumes are encouraged, and teams are picked so everyone plays and nobody sits the bench. The upstairs restaurant is open all evening and hosts a watch party for Detroit City's men's pro team afterwards; outside food and drink are not permitted. It names two contacts, a Detroit City FC operations assistant and the owner (a DMC/WSU general surgery physician), with their phone numbers and e-mail addresses (withheld in the extract), a QR code and link to a Google Form for registration, the openspineconsortium.com/celebrate-life page and two social handles.
