artifacts.title: Level Verification Bench
artifacts.readme_summary: Random-sample bench for checking the model's vertebral level names on decoded panels (page with its data file; its db rows are not copied). Copied at the owner's word after the first export held it back; the flagged string was base64 noise.
artifacts.date_evidence: Neither index.html nor the data file verify_data.js carries a date, run stamp or 'as of' line; the data rows hold no timestamps (keys: caption_consistent, confidence, decided_by, file, hard_caption, id, image_id, img, labels, n_boxes, panel_path, reversed, route).
artifacts.question: Is the vertebral level name the model gave each numbered box on a random sample of decoded panels right, wrong or undecidable when a person looks at the image?
artifacts.summary: An interactive bench that shows a random sample of decoded fluoroscopy panels, 179 panels holding 865 numbered vertebra boxes, and asks a person to mark each model-given level name as right, wrong or can't tell, typing the correct level where known. The page says the sample is random within each route and drawn with a fixed seed so the result is an unbiased estimate of accuracy, and that a set chosen by the model's own uncertainty could not serve that way; it calls the sample the measurement, not training data. Each panel card shows the route, whether the decode was caption-constrained or caption-free, what decided the names (model, caption, mate, hardware, vlm or anchor) and whether the panel was read bottom-up; a key marks a whole panel right at once, and verdicts save to the page's document store as verdicts/<id>. The export carries the page and its 4.2 MB data file but no verdicts: the counters stand at 0 / 0 and the accuracy reads as a dash.

key_claims.claim: The sample is 179 decoded panels with 865 vertebra boxes and is the measurement, not training data.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A random sample of decoded panels. 179 panels, 865 vertebrae. This is the measurement, not training data.

key_claims.claim: Because the sample is random within each route with a fixed seed, the verified accuracy is an unbiased estimate; a set chosen by the model's own uncertainty could not be used this way.

artifacts.summary: A gallery of every figure on disk at 20:12 on 22 September 2026 in spinesurg-ct-nnunet's paper/rsnai/figures on branch L6_Class: the tall composite fig1_story_tall.png (stacked at 19:31 by tools/fig_story_compose.py, not yet restacked), ten current row images (a to j) and three audit figures. Two rows (anatomy, fluoroscopic localisation) were re-rendered at 20:12 to remove the algebraic rule annotations. The captions describe the method: the off-by-one ambiguity of a lumbarised S1; the chain expose, detect, link, chain, count, confirm with only the shaded boxes learned; the count walking up two real VerSe columns (verse108 with 23 bodies, verse547 with 24 and a thirteenth thoracic); a four-exposure sweep stitched and counted from the sacrum; consecutive-window matching whose millimetre values are under review because verse_drr spacing is suspected about 15% short (checklist item A8); confirmation on a render with a 0.18 margin over one body off; fluoroscopic localisation readout; confirmation on Cios Fusion-styled frames finding a sixth lumbar vertebra at a weak 0.01 margin; the training corpus pictograms; the detector (1024 px, CSP backbone, PAN over three scales, decoupled head) and localiser (96 px crop plus target channel, ResNet-18, BiGRU over two to nine bodies, 27-level posterior); and a region-occlusion ablation at L3. The audit figures cover which training data contributes (the DeepFluoro question, text in SchwingNet/results/DATA_CONTRIBUTION.md), per-device C-arm card sampling with its saturation spikes, and the share of the learned joint distribution a frame reached (1.7–5.1% at the clip width in code, 99% with the typicality gate).

artifacts.notes: The page is a dated build report of the manuscript's figures, so most claims are measured against the figure files themselves rather than against data; the three result numbers (98.2 vs 92.5, 71.8, -2.1) are the artifact's own results but carry no n or interval in the text. It describes the method's mechanism (the sacral anchor count, the confirmation strip with the crop slid along the chain, the two networks with residual skips and a recurrence, the detector's training sources), hence schwingnet-method.

artifacts.title: Symphony and Beethoven Taxonomy Spec
artifacts.readme_summary: The spec of the Symphony and Beethoven taxonomy; here because the sort search found a SchwingNet term in it (Docs type, kept as Markdown; chips kept as text)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line under the title: "Oct 15, 2026 · @f"; the as-of verification dates throughout are also 2026-10-15 ("Verified from each project's repository or docs, 2026-10-15").
artifacts.question: What kind of software Symphony and Beethoven are, where they sit among their neighbors on a twelve-axis taxonomy, what they add that is unique, what GitHub Actions' free public minutes mean for them, and what is still unproven.
artifacts.summary: The spec places Symphony (a claim protocol, board and workers for Claude Code agents kept in a GitHub repository and run on GitHub Actions, with no server) and Beethoven (protocols, gates and agents for research on Wayne State's Slurm cluster) and the stack they are designed to form, which today meets nowhere in code. It proposes a twelve-axis taxonomy of agent systems, adding the one axis it says no published taxonomy has, cost model and payer, and places both systems and about twenty neighbors on it. It gathers the evidence of need (CooperBench's coordination gap, agent-driven research failures, metered CI costs), words six narrow uniqueness claims U1 to U6 after an adversarial search of 25 candidates, and sets out what GitHub's free unlimited standard runners on public repositories do and do not cover. It closes with fourteen risks, among them a push-guard directory bug found on 2026-10-15 and the pusher-written idle clock (finding F8), and ten research questions R1 to R10 with acceptance criteria. Every claim carries one of the artifact's own grades: Verified, Inferred, Reported or Open.

R2: Is the combination of mechanisms in section 8 unique, under a documented search of FSE, ICSE, ASE 2026, arXiv and GitHub topics?
R3: What does one coordination step cost, and which GitHub limit (1,000 requests an hour, the 100-run queue) binds first?
R4: Does the claim hold on github.com as on a local git server (second creation, descendant push, forced push, rename on release, the F8 clock)?
R5: Are Actions workers, benchmarks and a paid App inside GitHub's Actions terms?

artifacts.readme_summary: The sealed-repository standard for Beethoven's seven code repositories, who pins what from whom, and what still crosses a boundary (Docs type, kept as Markdown; the dependency diagram dropped, chips kept as text)

artifacts.question: How are Beethoven's seven code repositories sealed from one another, which repository pins what from which, and what still crosses a boundary?
artifacts.summary: The report states that all seven Beethoven code repositories (hpcworker, beethoven-sites, beethoven-extension, beethoven-desktop, beethoven-qa, beethoven-agents, beethoven-research) are now sealed under a five-rule standard merged in the hub as INTERFACES.md: each builds from its own tree, declares its exports and imports in interface/INTERFACE.json, takes another repository's work only as a pinned copy checked against an ORIGIN record, tests only against the published surface, and follows a fixed direction (qa, then agents, then research, never back). A table gives who offers what to whom, each repository's section says how it proves its export is the truth about its code (contract vectors, conformance and boundary tests), and a list names the three entries that still reach another checkout and why. Read-only neighbours (Beethoven for VS Code, the website, the two studies, spinesurg-ct-nnunet) were audited but not changed, with the high-weight crossings listed. The report leaves the owner two decisions: whether the VS Code edition gives up its own grid scripts for hpcworker's, and whether qa's vendor command should fetch through gh. It closes with the pull requests merged and what their gates showed, including fourteen client readers that disagreed with hpcworker's real output and two faults found in CrossHair 0.0.111.

artifacts.question: How does a lab paper run as a chain of files from a frozen pre-registration through grid jobs and a numbers manifest to the manuscript, and which data rules, grid rules and checklists hold that chain together?
artifacts.summary: A Docs page (kept as Markdown) that sets out how a lab project is staffed (lead, co-lead, members; senior scientist co-PI screens, senior clinical PI confirms clinical reads, the PI signs every freeze) and how a paper is produced so that a number enters the manuscript only through a recorded chain: PREREG.md frozen with its sha256, results files carrying a _run block, numbers_manifest.json, \RESULT{key} macros in the tex, and a reproduce target that fails on MISSING or MOVED. It fixes data rules that never bend (the five-criterion IRB umbrella HPR 2026-269, CTSpinoPelvic1K licences, a private-forever list including level-identification code, FluoroCap, weights, spinesurg-ct-nnunet and XRSpinoPelvic1K, credentials, personal data, label maps, volume orientation, zero-padded ids, two tracks), each with the incident that caused it. Fourteen grid rules with their incidents, a Slurm job template, Nextflow guidance for three-or-more-stage CPU pipelines, a numbers-checking procedure, rules for working with Claude (checkpoint block, no squeue polling beyond ten minutes, status computed by pipeline_state.py), handover and authorship rules, and three checklists follow. It ends with a table of ten gaps that are not yet true as of 2026-09-27, among them 167 bare numerals in the SchwingNet tables and 0 of 79 manifest keys carrying a Slurm job id.

artifacts.title: Secure Hybrid RDP Access: Spec and Setup Runbook
artifacts.readme_summary: Remote Desktop to the P50 only over Tailscale, with Duo MFA for every device but the owner's laptop (Docs type, kept as Markdown; the access-path diagram dropped, chips kept as text)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Sep 27, 2026 · @[the owner]'.
artifacts.question: How is Remote Desktop to the P50 workstation set up so that it is reachable only over Tailscale, with Duo MFA on every device except the owner's own laptop, and without any way to lock the owner out?
artifacts.summary: A spec and step-by-step runbook for Remote Desktop to the owner's P50 workstation: the P50 accepts RDP only over Tailscale, the owner's laptop signs in with the Windows password alone, every other device must also pass Duo MFA, and nothing on the P50 is reachable from the open internet. A table lists what changed from the original spec (no port forwarding instead of internet-exposed RDP guarded by Duo; a /32 bypass for the laptop instead of the whole 100.64.0.0/10 range; firewall and Tailscale access rules added; key expiry disabled only on the P50; Duo prompting only on RDP with bypass codes on paper). Five design rules are followed by prerequisites (Windows Pro or above, a Duo paid plan since Duo Free cannot do the bypass, a password logon, BitLocker key saved offline), a Windows 10 warning (6th-generation Intel CPU, Windows 10 extended support ending October 13, 2026), and five phases: prep, Tailscale on both machines, RDP with the firewall scoped to the tailnet, Duo Admin Panel policy, Duo install with RDP-only prompting, and a Tailscale grant restricting access to the owner's own devices. Six verification tests, a troubleshooting table and lockout recovery close it.

artifacts.title: Grid and cloud Claude workers: review
artifacts.readme_summary: Review of grid and cloud workers against industry practice, ten ranked fixes (Docs type, kept as Markdown)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Oct 21, 2026'; the state was 'read at 12:03 UTC, 21 Oct'.
artifacts.question: How do the grid and cloud Claude workers compare with industry practice, and which ten fixes are worth making, in what order?
artifacts.summary: A review of how the control panel starts, watches, stops and opens Claude workers on the Wayne State grid (a press runs grid-accounts.yml, one fixed ssh word to a forced-command gate, hpcworker submits one sbatch running Claude Code under Remote Control) and in GitHub Actions (workers.yml on the token pool). On 21 October the grid answered with framework 22, one worker online on node hao1 and account 1 signed in; no second worker has been started since that spends allocation. Against Runner Controller, Slurm, Kubernetes operators, hosted coding agents and Temporal, the design is on par for cancel, idempotency, coordination and credential scope, and behind on intake (a burst of presses loses one), tracking (state known only when asked), observability, error causes and key lifetime. Ten ranked fixes follow, the first five being durable request files, starting N workers in one word, pushing claims every 30 minutes and before TERM, a scheduled list every 15 minutes, and showing the shell's error. What was verified and what is not yet measured are listed.

key_claims.claim: On 21 October the grid answers with framework 22, one worker online on hao1 and account 1 (a Max subscription) signed in.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: the list run of 12:03 UTC (request verify22) succeeded and returned a `workers` array, one worker online on hao1, account 1 on a Max subscription.

key_claims.claim: GitHub keeps at most one waiting run per concurrency group, so a third quick press of Start replaces the second, which never runs.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The lost-press behaviour of rank 1 is GitHub's documented rule for concurrency groups; the workflow sets cancel-in-progress to false, which does not change it.

key_claims.claim: The gate's floor is 60 seconds for start, login and usage and 3 seconds for the other accounts words, one call at a time under a lock.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The gate's floor is read from its code: 60 seconds for start, login and usage, 3 seconds for the other accounts words, one call at a time under a lock.

key_claims.claim: A start by a name already running submits nothing.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: A start by a name already running submits nothing, from hpcworker's own check.

key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: covered by the panel's checks (grid tests G9 and G10, runs test R1, with mutants that each fail them) and by the template's tests with a fake ssh and git.

key_claims.claim: A grid worker busy for a day without pushing loses its claim to the board's 24-hour release.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The board releases a claim after 24 hours with no push, even when a grid worker is busy on it.

key_claims.claim: No port is open on the grid, no Claude credential leaves it, and git is the durable record of who works on what.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: No port is open on the grid, no Claude credential leaves it, a start by a name that is already running submits nothing, and git is the durable record of who works on what.

key_claims.claim: The design falls short in three places: lost or slowed requests, state known only when asked, and failures without causes.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: requests can be lost or slowed on the way in, it only finds out a worker's state when someone asks, and it does not say why a failure happened.

artifacts.question: How can the Beethoven extension switch between and update several Claude workers on the grid, one per claude.ai project, when the laptop cannot keep several Claude desktops signed in at once?
artifacts.summary: A plan answering the owner's request of 2026-10-21 to switch between and update projects through several Claude workers on the grid, driven from the browser through the Beethoven extension. It says most of the grid side exists: since hpcworker framework 22 the grid runs several named workers at once, each a separate Slurm job with its own Remote Control link and status, started with accounts start N NAME on a Claude account slot, and the control panel's Grid tab lists them; what is missing is on the Beethoven side, which knows one worker name and one project address. The design gives Beethoven a projects list in Settings (name, project address, grid worker, account slot), a chip switcher on the home screen with one tab per project, start-on-press through the portal shell, an Update press that fast-forwards the worker's workspace to main, and the same pairing stored on the grid in accounts.json so the control panel reads one record. The build order is four pull requests: hpcworker's project field and accounts list, Beethoven's list and switcher (a store release), the control panel's project column, then the workspace Update. Two open questions are not yet measured: whether two workers on one Claude account can each stay a separate environment, and whether a project's Work locally pairing survives a wall-time restart with --continue.

artifacts.summary: The page is the end-of-session handoff for Symphony, OpenSpineConsortium's coordination product for Claude Code agents on GitHub, with seven files attached: PLAN.md (eleven phases and fourteen owner questions), HANDOFF.md (the page as Markdown), session.md (the template's checkpoint), DESIGN-runtime.md (one public versioned runtime every copy calls, with an adversarial critique), DESIGN-qa-gate.md (a generic QA gate on GitHub's own tools, with a verification), RESEARCH-scale.md (the QA gate requirement, fewer moving parts, the CooperBench benchmark and an account pool) and free-or-paid.md (which GitHub features cost what per plan), plus one patch set aside. It records that symphony-protocol v0.4.1 was released on the owner's approval at 13:39 UTC, the first release through the new gate, fixing six of twelve defects the validation prototype found, and that the sync landed in all four consumers with the plugin at 0.1.10. It lists the owner's manual steps (limit organization secrets, delete five old test repositories, submit Symphony for Chrome, Beethoven tags and store upload, spine-program #72) and tells the next session to recheck every claim against GitHub first, then do the template's follow-up for 0.4.1, three small pull requests, the plan ladder memory and Phase 1 (the validation harness). The runtime design measures a whole-template copy at 145 files and 28,436 lines shrinking to 38 files and about 1,070, and its critique finds three unknowns, an understated blast radius, a privacy reversal and no simpler setup for adopters. The handoff also gives step-by-step instructions for starting the next session in a claude.ai Project with pasted project instructions and a first message.

key_claims.claim: A reusable-workflow call's secrets mapping is evaluated before any runner exists, so one account's token per session can be isolated; a dynamic lookup inside a step would put every secret on the runner.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Inferred, not measured: a dynamic lookup inside a step puts every secret the repository can see on that runner.

key_claims.claim: A bash bootstrap with CRLF line endings would block every Bash call on Windows, since a PreToolUse hook that exits 2 blocks the tool call.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Reproduced: `/tmp/.../crlf.sh` printed "syntax error near unexpected token" and exited 2.

key_claims.claim: beethoven-qa is private and proprietary with no licence, so no public repository can use an action or workflow it holds.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: gh api repos/OpenSpineConsortium/beethoven-qa --jq '{visibility,license}' gave {"visibility":"private","license":null}

key_claims.claim: The organization is on Enterprise Cloud, so every rule, review, environment and attestation is included on its private repositories; only the scanning add-ons cost extra and are free on its public repositories.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Your organization is on Enterprise Cloud, so every rule, review, environment and attestation is included in its private and internal repositories. Only the scanning add-ons cost extra

key_claims.claim: Push rulesets exist only for private and internal repositories, and with an empty bypass list they would block the owner too, so they do not close the self-judging hole.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Push rulesets exist only for private and internal repositories ... With `bypass_actors` empty, which the research itself recommends, the rule would also block [the owner].

key_claims.claim: Publishing the runtime would reverse a recorded privacy decision; the critique recommends a public repository that holds only releases.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The decision reads: "'Free to use' is not 'free access to the source' ... sdlc-start, which holds no file of it"

decisions.decision: Each release of symphony-protocol waits for the owner's approval in the environment release, fails closed without it, and the sync carries only a published release from the commit that raised main to its version (decision 5, symphony-protocol#12).
decisions.reason: a release reaches every copy, and today no person reviews it

decisions.decision: The owner approved the release of symphony-protocol v0.4.1, the first release through the gate.

A session merges any pull request once its checks are green, on the owner's standing permission in perpetuity, spine-program's too while Symphony is in its development phase; privacy pushes need no ask.

Releases were allowed without the owner's approval for the development phase, but no session can approve or publish one, so each release still waits for the owner's click until the owner tells a session in the owner's own words to switch the approval off in release.yml.
decisions.reason: the approval needs deployments: write, which a session's token lacks, and the cloud proxy refuses a session's release

decisions.decision: The safety check refused the session's attempts to switch the release approval off without the owner's own words.
decisions.reason: a change to the gate needs the owner's explicit words first

decisions.decision: Open core: the runtime, the protocol and the plugin public; the hosted parts (panel, account pool and switching, QA reports, analytics) a paid App; the template's private status no longer a moat.
One public, versioned runtime (symphony-protocol renamed symphony) holds all of Symphony's logic and every copy calls it through a few small files.
decisions.reason: so a copy can never fall behind and setup shrinks to callers and settings

decisions.decision: The update route for older copies is parked and the old test repositories are deleted and made fresh.
decisions.reason: the runtime replaces the update route

decisions.decision: Symphony Setup ticks the Actions box (Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests) in whole-template adoptions.
Workers and the coordinator come with protocol-only adoptions too, on the repository's own tests, with a default worker registered unless a box opts out.
The control panel is a site page plus a small stateless Cloudflare sign-in service.
One token for many Symphony repositories as an organization secret, never Beethoven's; the plugin goes to Anthropic's directory after the fresh test.
A QA report on every agent's change; few moving parts; a validation harness with concolic testing whose findings are fixed; the owner's accounts as one pool, then CooperBench.
Only people with write access queue work for a worker; the coordinator's tasks from an epic the owner marked keep todo, and its tidy's proposals wait for the owner.
decisions.reason: the Task form adds todo for anyone, and the next run works it on the owner's plan

decisions.decision: GitHub stops a worker changing what steers workers, by the qa check run from the default branch's copy and code-owner review on those paths.
decisions.reason: today's check runs the pull request's own scripts/check.sh, and the Claude App holds Workflows write

decisions.decision: The token in the organization secret is best from an account the owner never uses by hand; this is advice, never enforced.
decisions.reason: the workers share its five-hour window, but some people have only one Claude account

decisions.decision: At most 10 Claude runs a day per repository, coordinator included, set by a repository variable; none while the default branch is red or after three failures in a row.
decisions.reason: each six-hourly run or queued issue can start six 90-minute runs

decisions.decision: No settings-as-code app (issue #18).
decisions.reason: a dependency with admin rights on every repository it covers

decisions.decision: The owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator of the owner's, knowing the terms question; this never extends to contributors' credentials.
Beethoven repositories run no Symphony code and hold no Claude token; no ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateway.

Recommended, not yet decided: publish releases only, not development; the moving tag drives background jobs only while the check, hooks and Claude jobs run a reviewed pin; v1 moves only through a dedicated release App approved in the web UI.
decisions.owner: the session (critique of the runtime design)
decisions.reason: a bad release on a moving tag could write a persistent bootstrap into every copy and instruct every session

open_questions: Questions 6 to 14 of PLAN.md: the runtime's licence and what is public; how copies follow releases (moving tag versus reviewed pin); fewer moving parts (delete the webhook stage, retire the sweep, a canary repository); the Actions box in protocol-only adoptions; code scanning on private repositories; SymphonyBoard's Actions permission and narrowed installation; which repositories the pool may reach; coordbench#6's grid route; piloting the claim protocol in beethoven-qa.

Six validation findings left: F2 (overlap told twice), F4 (clerk deals one issue to two workers), F7 (lease push onto another's claim), F8 (idleness from the pusher's commit date), F9 (does a draft hear 'main moved'), F12 ('main moved' lost when a newer run cancels).
Whether claude-code-action's OIDC token exchange accepts a job defined in another organization's reusable workflow, and which workflow file its validation compares.
Whether $/ resolves across organizations in practice, and how nested permissions behave for a narrower caller shape.
Whether an approval-required pull_request run on the same head holds the merge beside a dispatched check named check.

Whether secrets[...] with a computed name works in a reusable-workflow call's secrets mapping, whether a run under every threshold emits a rate_limit_event, and whether cache-mode: write works on issues-triggered runs.
How many outside copies of Symphony exist (the proxy refuses the App's installation listing).
Whether the two largest CooperBench flash images fit a 14 GB runner, and concurrency beyond two sessions per subscription token.
Whether Secret Protection or Code Quality is licensed on the organization, and whether the Pro and Team prices are current.
The bootstrap's start-up time in a cloud session and whether a long board keeps a SessionStart output under the 10,000-character cap.
Whether the organization and repository names must become part of v1 given GitHub supports no redirects for actions or reusable workflows.

artifacts.question: In what phases, each with a measured gate, should the Beethoven research engine be built on top of hpcworker and beethoven-extension, and what must the owner decide first?
artifacts.summary: A six-phase roadmap for turning the two Beethoven repositories, hpcworker (framework 11) and beethoven-extension (12.0.0), from a transport layer into a research engine. Phase 0 is one probe job that decides whether the inner loop can be headless claude -p on the student's own login from a batch job; phases 1 to 5 add one headless run, a chained-Slurm-job outer loop with a run ledger, REFORMS gates enforced by code, paper and archive steps with a student-pressed Publish, and scale to two concurrent projects and a second site. A table maps each REFORMS control to its phase and enforcement, with module numbers not yet checked against Kapoor et al. 2024. The repositories' standing rules (no credential handling, nothing on the login node beyond one sbatch, 60 s polling, node-local temp, bash 4.2 and Python 3.6) shape the design. Six decisions are left to the owner with a recommendation each, and the notebook's proposals that the plan rejects are listed.

artifacts.title: The Dollar-per-Feature Ladder
artifacts.readme_summary: What the template costs at each price rung, verified 9 October 2026 (Docs type, kept as Markdown)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Oct 9, 2026 · @[the owner]'; body says 'the ladder below was verified against GitHub's and Anthropic's own pages on Oct 9, 2026' and 'on 2026-10-09'.
artifacts.question: What does running the sdlc-template (the shared-repository, agent-driven software project) cost at each GitHub and Claude price rung, and what named feature does each dollar above the bottom rung buy?
artifacts.summary: The page argues that the template runs whole for $17 a month (one Claude Pro seat billed annually plus a public repository on GitHub Free), that the GitHub bill at that rung is $0 by construction because an account with no stored payment method is halted at the quota rather than billed, and that GitHub Pro and Team both include the same 3,000 private-repo CI minutes, so money above the bottom rung buys governance and usage rather than compute until Enterprise's 50,000 minutes. It lays out a five-rung ladder (Free+Pro, +GitHub Pro, Team+Claude Team, premium seats or Max, Enterprise) with what each genuinely adds, describes three pull requests (#3, #5, #7) that turned the protocol's prose into mechanism, and explains the zero-inference core (native settings beat workflows, workflows beat inference). It refuses to price the Enterprise tier because Claude Enterprise's pricing could not be verified. A verification section reports a 103-agent research run on 2026-10-09 with 21 sources, 95 claims, the top 25 verified by three votes each, 23 confirmed and 2 refuted, and a 'Turning it on' checklist with the first item done.

artifacts.question: How does one use the Symphony and Beethoven taxonomy spec: run the deep research that checks it, test a claim, place any other tool in the taxonomy, explain the approach to grant reviewers, engineers and lab leads, and keep the spec current?
artifacts.summary: A companion to the taxonomy spec (linked as a claude.ai artifact) that holds procedures rather than claims: what to read first, which claims were already checked against primary sources on 2026-10-15, and a three-pass deep-research procedure whose first pass is a long prompt to paste into claude.ai Research because the project's cloud sessions cannot reach docs.github.com, arxiv.org and other hosts. It gives a six-step method for testing a claim (write it with its scope, write the refutation first, search by mechanism, run it on a scratch repository, record a null search, narrow or drop), a ranked table of which sources give which grade (Verified, Inferred, Reported, Open), and a twelve-axis worksheet plus five mechanisms (a) to (e) for placing any tool, worked through for unsorry (agenticsnz/unsorry at 029d328b), which scores one yes and three partials and so does not refute uniqueness claim U1. Section 6 gives the argument in order (need, mechanism, economics, evidence, limits) with tailored paragraphs for grant reviewers, engineers and lab leads, a table of what to say and not say about free GitHub Actions minutes, and honest answers to engineers' questions (only a claim's creation is enforced on GitHub; idleness is read from the pusher's committer date; F8 is written but not merged). Section 7 lists seven recipes for combining Symphony and Beethoven with other software (security gates, beethoven-qa as a qa lane, the Claude-free core in a Beethoven repository, other agents under the claim, merge queue, workflow managers, Actions as control plane), each marked works today, planned, chosen or not tried. Section 8 says what to re-check when prices, terms, releases or neighbors change, and section 9 is a glossary.

artifacts.readme_summary: The plan of 2026-10-08 for the repository as every account's shared plane: Route A against Route B, the tools to lean on, phases and risks (Docs type, kept as Markdown; one embedded widget dropped, chips kept as text)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line under the title: "Oct 8, 2026 · @f". The body also records later events: "sized on 2026-10-09" and "On 2026-10-09 [the owner] chose GitHub Issues".
artifacts.question: Should the shared-plane SDLC be built by expanding Claude Swap Cloud (Route A) or as a focused utility on top of what already exists (Route B), and in what phases?
artifacts.summary: The plan recommends Route B: build a small standard-library materializer that turns a cswap Project export into repository files (CLAUDE.md, docs/memory/, docs/history/, docs/project.md), leave the Claude Swap Cloud extension and bridge unchanged, and run the unattended export through a routine inside the Project rather than any browser scheduler, which the Consumer Terms forbid. It sets each account's claude.ai Project as a thin pointer to the repository and leans on GitHub Issues, branch protection, a board-regenerating Action, Anthropic-run routines and cloud threads instead of bespoke services. A table maps each architectural need to an existing tool. Six phases (0 to 5, an hour to two days each) each end with a measurement on the real claude-swap Project; on 2026-10-09 the owner chose GitHub Issues and asked for the repository side first as a template repository with no export or import in its first layer. Risks listed include the terms, multi-account use of one repository, routine caps, the lossy prompt route, one-way memory flow, instruction drift, branch protection on a private repository, keys in Actions and unpublished routes.

artifacts.readme_summary: What cswap and Claude Swap Cloud could export and import of a claude.ai Project on 2026-10-08, and the gaps (Docs type, kept as Markdown; chips kept as text)

artifacts.question: What can cswap and Claude Swap Cloud already export and import of a claude.ai Project, and what gaps remain before the multi-account SDLC can be built on them?
artifacts.summary: The spec inventories every primitive in the claude-swap repository that moves or holds a claude.ai Project's knowledge (the export and import browser scripts, cswap project-move in its folder, branch-carrier and auto forms, the Chrome extension and its bridge, cswap teleport, the handoff note, the checkpoint and the read-only account registry) and maps each Project field (name, instructions, topic, memory, files, repositories, settings, members, threads, sessions) to the route it is read from, the file it lands in, the request that writes it back and whether the round trip is whole. It then measures these against what the SDLC architecture (documents 22, 23 and 25 and the plan of 2026-10-08) needs: CLAUDE.md from the instructions, docs/memory/ from the memory, docs/history/ from the conversations, a deterministic handoff brief and an unattended export. It finds nothing writes instructions into CLAUDE.md or memory under docs/memory/, the memory write precondition has never been seen live, exports are non-deterministic with no checksums, and no unattended export is possible under Anthropic's terms except a lossy routine-run prompt route. It closes with the binding constraints: no scripting of claude.ai on a schedule, Projects belong to one account, every account signs in itself, trust boundaries and store rules stay, no new runtime dependencies, deterministic checkpoints, and platform limits on routine fires and file sizes.

artifacts.question: Where does Symphony stand, by design, against every other way of coordinating coding agents, and what may honestly be claimed for it before any outcome is measured?
artifacts.summary: The Doc sets Symphony, a GitHub repository acting as the coordinator of Claude Code agents with no server of its own, beside four kinds of system: work-queue coordinators (gh-aw, unsorry, openai/symphony, CCPM, Beads and Gas Town, paperclip, agentic-setup, Orbi, aeon), vendor-hosted agents, single-session orchestration and agent frameworks. Two tables apply the manual's two questions (what stops a second agent taking the same work, what frees an unfinished claim) and record where each runs, who pays and what was read at which commit on 2026-10-15. It argues Symphony is better by design in three respects, graded Inferred: one claim rule for sessions, routines and Actions agents on a flat-rate subscription, an idle claim released with its work kept, and a shipped library checked over every interleaving against an oracle with mutants. It then lists where Symphony is not better or not yet (no outcome evidence, pre-release 0.4.1, the claim enforced only at creation, the idle clock read from the committer date, scale unmeasured), what not to claim, one paragraph per audience and a full sources section.

decisions.decision: The three uniqueness claims are worded narrowly and graded Inferred, since unsorry has the board in CI and looser forms of the other mechanisms.
decisions.reason: A search that finds nothing cannot verify; the spec names what would refute each claim.

decisions.decision: coordbench's numbers stay out of the grant until the owner lifts the hold.
decisions.reason: The harness audit found 11 of 40 runs spoiled; figures are not reportable until reruns and the pre-registered full run complete.

decisions.decision: Orbi and aeon are left out of the head-to-head tables; Claude Code Projects and Claim Plane are named for completeness only.
decisions.reason: They have no claim between workers (Orbi, aeon), no shared claim across accounts (Projects) or serialize almost every execution (Claim Plane).

decisions.decision: Do not claim an atomic claim on the forge, serverless coordination in Actions, free coordination on a public repository, the subscription token in Actions, one issue one branch one PR, free or unlimited agents, 'nothing else does this', Anthropic's approval, a benchmark win, or the Symphony and Beethoven stack.
decisions.reason: Each has prior art or is untrue as a headline.

decisions.decision: Better means better designed, not measured better, until an outcome is shown.
decisions.reason: No peer-reviewed study or benchmark compares the protocol with one agent at a matched budget.

open_questions: R1: whether the protocol beats one agent at a matched budget (coordbench run in progress, figures held).
R2: the systematic search for competitors has not been run; two leads of the 14-query search are unread.
R3: where API limits bind at scale is unmeasured; the library has no retry on 429.
R5 and R6: GitHub's Actions terms tie runner use to the repository's own project, and Anthropic advises an API key for a shared secret; bare mode for claude -p does not read the token.
R10: the name collides with openai/symphony.
Whether ordering overlapping work by file reduces conflicts is unmeasured.
Whether CooperBench's published counts go in the grant is the owner's call.
The idle-clock fix (#35) leaves one gap, a claim's first push, and is unreleased.
Reproduction and fix of the push guard reading the hook's working directory (risk 12) and of a reopened issue dealt to nobody (risk 14) are queued.

artifacts.title: Symphony in brief
artifacts.readme_summary: What Symphony is, how it works, its 17 guarantees and what is not measured yet, as of 2026-10-14 (Docs type, kept as Markdown; the lifecycle diagram dropped, chips kept as text)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line under the title: "Oct 14, 2026" with the author chip; the body says "On symphony-protocol's main today (b5f098d, after F15 and F16 merged this evening)".
artifacts.question: What is Symphony, how does it coordinate many Claude Code workers on one GitHub repository, which of its 17 guarantees are checked, what does it not promise, and how does it stand against CooperBench and other agent coding work as of 2026-10-14?
artifacts.summary: Symphony lets many Claude Code workers share one GitHub repository using only GitHub's own objects: issues are the queue, the first push of a branch claude/N is the lock, and a pull request is the only way work lands. A board on the branch board, a coordinator step in the same run (releases claims idle 24 hours, tells overlapping work its landing order) and fences (a push guard hook, branch protection, CI's protocol check) run around six steps: queue, pick, claim, work in the open, finish, release. Of its 17 bookkeeping guarantees, 12 hold on symphony-protocol main b5f098d, 2 hold only if commit dates are honest, 1 is known broken (G7, repeat overlap notices), 1 is partly checked and 1 not checked, by bounded search of small worlds, 59 caught mutants and 20,970 generated push commands, which is checking and not proof. It does not promise correct code, progress, speed from parallel work, semantic conflict detection, fair idle times or protection from anyone with write access. Against CooperBench (Sonnet 4.5 fell from 47.1% solo to 25.8% as a pair; the authors' later ablation got 56% with a shared git remote and 62% with a team) Symphony is the opposite, shared and continuously merged design, but coordbench's pre-registered 50-pair run has not happened, so no outcome is measured yet. A table sets it beside SWE-bench, MetaGPT, ChatDev, Anthropic's C compiler experiment, Claude Code agent teams, Anthropic's multi-agent research system and Cursor's long-running agents.

artifacts.title: Shared multi-account Claude project: plan
artifacts.readme_summary: The plan of 2026-10-08 that became Symphony: the repository as the shared plane, claims by branch push, a coordinator (Docs type, kept as Markdown; the architecture diagram dropped, chips kept as text)
artifacts.date_evidence: Byline 'Oct 8, 2026' and the sources line 'All opened on 2026-10-08.'
artifacts.question: How can several Claude accounts work on one project as a coordinated whole when no Claude product shares a Project, an agent or a memory across accounts?
artifacts.summary: The plan says to build around the repository, not around a shared Project, because a Project belongs to one account and no Claude product lets one account's agent talk live to another's. The repository holds code, rules and shared memory; Linear holds the queue; a task is claimed by pushing a branch named after its issue, which git accepts only once; the open PR is the progress and a merged PR plus a Done issue is the record. A coordinator routine on the owner's main account wakes on PR events, on pushes to main through a GitHub Action, and hourly, releasing claims idle for 24 hours, flagging overlapping PRs and rewriting a STATE.md board. Shared memory is one fact per file under docs/memory/ with an index, changed in the same PR as the work. A nine-step setup and a failure-mode table, drawn from CooperBench and other sources, close it, with a warning that running several subscription accounts as one swarm is a grey zone after reported bans in February 2026.

artifacts.title: Moving Beethoven for VS Code onto hpcworker
artifacts.readme_summary: The plan for the VS Code edition to become a client of hpcworker on the grid (Docs type, kept as Markdown; chips kept as text)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line "Oct 7, 2026 · @[the owner]" and the status note "On 2026-10-07 at 22:33Z [the owner] deferred the move"; other dates mentioned are earlier (2026-09-27, 2026-09-28, 2026-09-29, 2026-10-03, 2026-10-05).
artifacts.question: What would it take for Beethoven for VS Code to run its grid workers through the lab's shared hpcworker instead of its own grid scripts, and what must the owner decide before any code is written?
artifacts.summary: A plan, deferred by the owner on 2026-10-07, for Beethoven for VS Code to stop shipping its own ten grid scripts and become a client of the lab's shared hpcworker on the Wayne State grid, as the browser and desktop editions already are. It reads both code bases at pinned commits (beethoven-vscode 631226e, hpcworker e77863c) and finds that starting, stopping, status, the log, the Claude sign-in folder and the Remote Control consent carry over, while hpcworker lacks four things VS Code relies on: the Ask request channel, per-worker sizes and GPUs, the Remote-SSH sysroot lines, and GitHub and Hugging Face tokens. It flags four things to know now, among them a credential path in VS Code 5.0.0 by which an unchecked result id can return the Claude credential file to the laptop's Claude, and a lab-access gap by which a VS Code student not on the access service's roster loses the lab folder at every sync. It sets out a side-by-side table of every grid feature, an eleven-step order of work across hpcworker, beethoven-sites, beethoven-vscode and the hub (framework 18 and 19, VS Code 6.0.0 and 7.0.0), what already set-up students keep, the risks, and fourteen decisions for the owner with a recommended answer each. Nothing on the grid is deleted at any step, and many behaviours are marked not yet measured.

key_claims.claim: The move is feasible but not a quick swap: hpcworker covers start, stop, status and log but lacks four things VS Code students rely on (Ask, worker sizes, Remote-SSH lines, tokens).
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The move can be done, but it is not a quick swap. hpcworker already covers starting, stopping and watching a worker, but it lacks four things VS Code students rely on.

key_claims.claim: The owner deferred the move on 2026-10-07 because he is the only user of the VS Code edition and nothing else depends on it; VS Code keeps its grid scripts for now.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: On 2026-10-07 at 22:33Z [the owner] deferred the move, since he is the only person using the VS Code edition and nothing else in the ecosystem depends on it.

key_claims.claim: VS Code 5.0.0 has a credential path: result and its relay check neither worker name nor request id, so the id ../../../claude/.credentials returns the student's Claude credential file to the laptop's Claude; found by reading, not run.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: So the id `../../../claude/.credentials` returns the student's Claude credential file to the laptop's Claude. That breaks the rule that Beethoven never relays a credential.

key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The grid then runs `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions`. hpcworker's contract refuses that mode, and the plan drops it.

artifacts.summary: A step-by-step runbook for the owner, refreshed on 2026-10-08 for release 0.2.0.773 of the Claude Swap Cloud Chrome extension. Step 1, moving claude-swap and claude-swap-privacy to OpenSpineConsortium, was done on 2026-10-06 and the repository renamed claude-swap-cloud on 2026-10-07, so the owner starts at Step 2: create the store item from CI's zip (124,457 bytes), fill the twelve listing fields, the privacy tab (single purpose, per-permission justifications, remote code No, four data-usage boxes, PRIVACY.md version 15), distribution (Free, Unlisted, all regions) and test instructions (403 of 500 characters), then submit. Before submitting, cswap must be published on PyPI (pending publisher, tag v0.27.0b1) because the reviewer installs it with uv tool install. artifacts.title: Claude Chat vs. Claude Code: Architectural Analysis of Interface-Exclusive Capabilities
artifacts.readme_summary: Analysis of what Claude Chat can do that Claude Code cannot, and the reverse (Docs type, kept as Markdown)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line 'Oct 3, 2026 · @[the owner]'; closing section: 'Every product claim above was checked against Anthropic's documentation as published on October 3, 2026'.
artifacts.question: What can Claude Chat do that Claude Code cannot, and the reverse, and how should the two surfaces be combined in one working procedure?
artifacts.summary: A Docs-type analysis dated 3 October 2026 comparing Claude Chat (claude.ai/chat and the consumer apps) with Claude Code (one harness shipped through the CLI, the IDE extensions, cloud sessions at claude.ai/code, the GitHub Action and the Agent SDK). It first corrects the prompt's taxonomy: claude.ai/code is not the CLI, and three of the six features the prompt called exclusive (artifacts, vision, MCP) are shared, differing in ingestion path, scale and control plane rather than by a hard boundary. Chat's exclusives are the in-conversation preview runtime, server-side Project knowledge with retrieval mode and the hosted AI-powered artifact runtime billed to each viewer; Claude Code's are read/write/execute on the user's own machine, the terminal error loop against the real toolchain, hooks and permission rules, headless use and multi-session orchestration. It documents the agent loop, the tool set with its output limits, MCP transports, scopes and security, the data flow and retention by plan, and a set of workflow scenarios graded trivial, possible or impossible on each surface. It closes with a hybrid standard operating procedure (design and communicate in Chat; plan, build and verify in Claude Code; hand off through a committed spec, a pull request and a published page, with headless glue for recurring steps) and a sources table, flagging three statements as inferences rather than documented facts.

artifacts.title: Claude Code on a Slurm + Apptainer Cluster with a Consumer Subscription: Implementation Playbook
artifacts.readme_summary: Playbook for running Claude Code on a Slurm and Apptainer cluster with a consumer subscription (Docs type, kept as Markdown)
artifacts.date_evidence: Header line under the title reads "Oct 3, 2026" followed by the author's byline; the closing section says "Facts about Claude Code were checked against Anthropic's documentation on October 3, 2026."
artifacts.question: How can one person run Claude Code on a shared Slurm cluster inside an Apptainer image, authenticated by their own consumer subscription, within Anthropic's terms, with safe credentials, hard guardrails and batch runs that resume across job windows?
artifacts.summary: A dated implementation playbook for running Claude Code on a shared Slurm cluster inside a read-only Apptainer image, authenticated by one person's consumer (Pro or Max) subscription. It fixes four compliance conditions (one user one account, unmodified binary, no intermediation, no limit evasion), keeps regulated data off a consumer plan, and gives complete scripts: site discovery into site.env, a container definition that pins the Claude Code binary, relocation of all Claude Code state to scratch, a Slurm client passthrough with a submit-shim fallback, a launcher (claude-hpc), and two credentials (a one-year setup token for batch, a /login credential for interactive and Remote Control sessions). Guardrails are three layers: managed settings baked into the image (deny rules, timeouts, a 16G tool memory cap, sandbox off), a user settings allow list, and a PreToolUse guard hook; a CLAUDE.md blueprint, a slurm-operator subagent and a slurm-submit skill enforce cluster etiquette (job caps, measured resource requests, no sbatch --wrap). Three execution patterns are scripted: an interactive srun allocation, a persistent tmux workspace running claude remote-control, and a resumable claude -p pipeline that sizes itself to the Slurm window, resumes by session id and turns a usage-limit hit into a delayed resubmission. It closes with a version table of gated features, a source table of Anthropic documentation, and names two inferences to validate on site.

key_claims.claim: The deployment is permitted under Anthropic's terms as long as four conditions hold: one person's subscription authenticates only that person's sessions, the binary runs unmodified, no one else's work is routed through the account, and nothing evades usage limits.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: This deployment is permitted as long as four things stay true: one person's subscription authenticates only that person's sessions, the Claude Code binary runs unmodified

key_claims.claim: Anthropic's documentation describes the claude setup-token credential as intended for CI and non-interactive environments.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: intended "for CI pipelines, scripts, or other environments where interactive browser login isn't available"

key_claims.claim: Most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly, and Claude Code needs api.anthropic.com on every turn, so jobs must run on a partition with egress or through the site proxy.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly; Claude Code needs `api.anthropic.com` on every turn

key_claims.claim: CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in the environment takes precedence over .credentials.json, which lets the launcher choose the credential by injecting or omitting the token file.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` in the environment wins over `.credentials.json`, so the launcher injects the token file only when `CLAUDE_HPC_AUTH` is `token`

key_claims.claim: A headless -p run started after the /login access token has expired has been reported not to refresh it, which is why batch runs use the setup token.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: a headless `-p` run started after the access token has already expired has been reported not to refresh it (issue #50743, v2.1.114, 401 `authentication_error`)

key_claims.claim: The setup token is valid for one year and can only make model requests; it cannot open Remote Control or use claude.ai connectors.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: valid for one year; it can only make model requests (no Remote Control, no claude.ai connectors)

key_claims.claim: Subscription limits are per account, so parallel sessions on many nodes draw down one budget proportionally faster; the structure is a rolling five-hour window plus weekly caps.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: eight parallel sessions on eight nodes draw down one budget eight times faster. The structure has two layers: a rolling five-hour session window, and weekly caps

key_claims.claim: Rotating accounts or pooling tokens to widen the usage window is prohibited by Anthropic's terms; a workload that needs more than one subscription's window belongs on an API key.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit

key_claims.claim: Deny rules in managed settings are evaluated before ask and allow rules and cannot be re-enabled by user or project files; a Read deny also blocks Edit and Write on the same path.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Deny rules are evaluated before ask and allow rules, so nothing in a user or project file can re-enable them, and a `Read` deny also blocks `Edit` and `Write` on the same path

key_claims.claim: Claude Code's bubblewrap sandbox cannot normally nest inside an unprivileged Apptainer, so the sandbox is off and the container is the isolation layer.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: The sandbox is off because Claude Code's bubblewrap sandbox cannot normally nest inside an unprivileged Apptainer; the container itself is the isolation layer

key_claims.claim: Remote Control started with only the setup token fails; it needs the /login credential.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Remote Control with only the setup token fails with `Remote Control requires a claude.ai subscription`

key_claims.claim: The Slurm client passthrough and the nested-sandbox option are inferences to validate on each cluster, not documented behaviour.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Two things are inference rather than documentation and should be validated on your cluster: the Slurm client passthrough ... and the `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` option

key_claims.claim: Nothing in Claude Code sets a wall-clock limit on the agent as a whole; that limit must come from Slurm and the job script.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Nothing in Claude Code sets a wall-clock limit on the agent as a whole; that limit comes from Slurm and from the job script.

key_claims.claim: Bash permission rules are prefix matches and Claude Code strips wrappers such as timeout and xargs before matching.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Claude Code strips wrappers such as `timeout 30` and `xargs` before matching, so `Bash(pytest*)` also covers `timeout 600 pytest -q`

key_claims.claim: Anthropic's documentation describes generating the setup token but not revoking one.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Anthropic's documentation describes generating the token but not revoking one.

key_claims.claim: The facts about Claude Code in the playbook were checked against Anthropic's documentation on 2026-10-03, and several features are version-gated.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: Facts about Claude Code were checked against Anthropic's documentation on October 3, 2026. Several features this playbook relies on are version-gated

key_claims.claim: A 4-hour batch job inside a 4.5-hour limit with a 15-minute margin gives the agent a 3h45m budget, close to one five-hour window of ordinary use on the larger plans.
key_claims.evidence_in_artifact: a 4-hour job inside a 4.5-hour limit with a 15-minute margin leaves the agent a 3h45m budget, which is close to one five-hour window of ordinary use on the larger plans

decisions.decision: Batch and non-interactive runs authenticate with the one-year setup token; interactive and Remote Control sessions use a full /login credential.
decisions.reason: a headless -p run started after the access token has expired has been reported not to refresh it (issue #50743), and /login is the only credential that can open Remote Control or publish artifacts

decisions.decision: The Claude Code bubblewrap sandbox is switched off in managed settings; the Apptainer container is the isolation layer.
decisions.reason: the bubblewrap sandbox cannot normally nest inside an unprivileged Apptainer

decisions.decision: One account per user, no account rotation, no pooled tokens; a workload needing more than one subscription's window goes to an API key.
decisions.reason: rotating accounts or pooling tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit

decisions.decision: Regulated data (PHI, export-controlled, GDPR special categories) stays off a consumer plan; use an API key, a Team or Enterprise seat, or a cloud-provider route for that work.
decisions.reason: on Free, Pro and Max plans the account's Help improve Claude setting decides whether coding sessions are used for training

decisions.decision: The image contains no credentials; each user mints their own token on their laptop and stores it 0600 on their own scratch, never in .bashrc, a job script, an sbatch --export line or a module file.
decisions.reason: the token is a bearer credential for the whole subscription and one user, one account must stay mechanically true on a shared cluster

decisions.decision: Default to --model sonnet and medium effort for implementation runs; reserve Opus-class models for plan mode.
decisions.reason: in plan mode turns are few and reasoning matters; subscription limits are drawn per token per turn

decisions.decision: Only the slurm-operator subagent submits, monitors or cancels jobs; other subagents never call sbatch, srun, salloc or scancel.
decisions.reason: the guard hook, the permission rules and the instructions then apply at a single point, and an implementer subagent cannot queue jobs as a side effect of testing

decisions.decision: Non-interactive runs add --permission-mode dontAsk.
decisions.reason: it turns every would-be prompt into a denial the model can see and route around instead of a hang

decisions.decision: Host Slurm binaries are bound into /opt/slurm-bin rather than over /usr/bin.
decisions.reason: so the container's own tools are never shadowed

decisions.decision: The image base is rockylinux:9.
decisions.reason: it matches the RHEL family most university clusters run, so host Slurm binaries bound in load against a compatible glibc

decisions.decision: Jobs are submitted from a job-script file under jobs/, never with sbatch --wrap.
decisions.reason: so the script is reviewable and re-runnable

decisions.decision: A usage-limit hit in a batch window is a scheduled resubmission with --begin=now+5hours and --resume, not a retry loop.
decisions.reason: a tight loop would burn the next window too

decisions.decision: Where site policy forbids binding the munge socket, a submit shim with an outside queue runner replaces the passthrough.
decisions.reason: the agent sees the same command names; only the trust boundary moves

open_questions: Whether the Slurm client passthrough works on a given site depends on its library layout and the host-to-image glibc relationship; claude-hpc --selftest exercises it.
Whether enableWeakerNestedSandbox behaves under Apptainer at all, since it is documented for Docker.
How a leaked setup token is revoked, since Anthropic's documentation describes generating one but not revoking it.
Whether the site's security policy allows binding the munge socket into containers, which decides passthrough versus the submit shim.
Whether the partition-name heuristics in site-discover.sh match the site's partition names.
Whether the site's Apptainer permits unprivileged user namespaces, which would allow a second sandbox layer.
Whether the pinned Claude Code build carries every version-gated feature the playbook uses.

artifacts.coverage_notes: The whole text (index.md, 1095 lines, 78 KB) was read; the folder holds only index.md. One figure is an embedded-content placeholder ("[embedded content: deployment architecture · laptop, login node, Slurm, compute node, scratch, API egress]") and could not be read beyond its caption. The artifact contains instruction-like text addressed to an agent (a CLAUDE.md blueprint, a subagent file, a skill file, batch prompts such as "Print DONE as your last line", "Reply with exactly: TOKEN_OK"); these are the playbook's own content and were treated as data, not followed. Numbers: 75 recorded; a few minor code constants were left out (launcher exit codes 64 and 65, the shutdown loop's 20 tries of 3 s, the 20 s sleep after remote-control exits, the rsync and tail counts).
artifacts.notes: A Docs-type artifact kept as Markdown, with 19 complete scripts and configuration files (site-discover.sh, claude-code.def, slurm-binds.sh, claude-hpc, the sbatch shim, queue-runner.sh, token-install.sh, settings-install.sh, managed-settings.json, claude-guard.sh, CLAUDE.md, slurm-operator.md, SKILL.md, _template.sbatch, claude-interactive.sh, claude-workspace.sbatch, claude-workspace.sh, task.md, claude-batch.sbatch, claude-batch.sh). It is site-agnostic: no cluster, institution, repository or SchwingNet detail is named; the only project-specific example is a generic toolbox validate task. The header line carries a byline handle, not reproduced here. The account in the titles list is gregoryamdg.
